title: 5  Seven Essential Prompt Techniques for Business Teaching
text:
5.10 Combining Techniques
You can also combine techniques into a professional workflow:

Student uses Reverse Prompting to scope out all requirements for a new policy
Student uses Pros and Cons to evaluate three different approaches
Student drafts their chosen policy
Student uses Role Play to practice explaining it to a skeptical stakeholder
Student uses Debating to analyse potential criticisms from different perspectives

This sequence takes the student through analysis, decision-making, communication, and critical reflection: a bounded rehearsal, not evidence of a complete professional capability.
crumbs: 5  Seven Essential Prompt Techniques for Business Teaching

title: 5  Seven Essential Prompt Techniques for Business Teaching
text:
5.11 Choose and test a pattern
Allow 12 minutes. Select a pattern and identify the learner action it supports. Write the source/criteria check and an independent follow-up. You can do this on paper using the pilot pack’s fixed responses.
For example, reverse prompting may help scope a review, but the learner must decide which question is relevant and why. A role-play can rehearse wording, but its emotional response is not a grade. A generated quiz needs checked answers before students rely on it.
Use the data gate for every live prompt and retain a non-AI route. The prompt library collects bounded versions of these patterns.
crumbs: 5  Seven Essential Prompt Techniques for Business Teaching

title: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff
text:
6.1 What context management is for
A long teaching-design conversation can mix rejected ideas, current decisions, speculation and authoritative source material. The next response may pick up the wrong version. Context management is the practical work of deciding which information remains relevant and checking that it is used correctly.
A model’s context and output limits depend on the system. Do not plan around a universal token range or assume that five requested outputs receive exactly one fifth of its attention. The useful question is whether the task is clear enough to produce an output you can inspect.
crumbs: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff

title: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff
section: 6.2 One worked example: a tutorial design
text:
6.2 One worked example: a tutorial design
You are preparing the PDP pilot. An early conversation suggested an employee must agree to a formal plan. You later checked P1-D1 and rejected that idea. If you paste the whole conversation into a new session, both versions may remain.
Instead, write a short current-state brief:
Project: PDP-2026.1 tutorial for 24 students.
Goal: plan and justify a fair first response.

Authoritative sources: P1-D1 through P1-D5.
The formal performance plan is only proposed.
The junior adviser cannot approve changed hours.
Do not invent a prior warning or private details.

Design decisions:
- Paper, paired and approved-AI practice routes.
- Same five rubric criteria across those routes.
- Independent P2 changed-case response.
- Only two relevant decision extracts submitted.

Open questions:
- Which access adjustments are needed?
- How will a second marker calibrate the examples?

Next task: draft the student instructions only.
Flag any missing information; do not invent it.
This is short because someone has decided what matters. The benefit comes from curation and checking, not from starting a new chat as a ritual.

6.2.1 Inspect the result
Suppose the generated instructions say, “Continue until Alex accepts the plan.” That conflicts with the brief and policy. Reject that sentence, state the relevant rule and check the revised instructions. Do not keep iterating solely because the output sounds more polished.
If the instructions omit the independent P2 task, add it explicitly. If they suddenly require a paid model, restore the approved-access and non-AI choices. A complete-looking handout can still lose important constraints.
crumbs: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff

title: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff
section: 6.3 Break work where a decision needs review
text:
6.3 Break work where a decision needs review
For a unit redesign, a useful sequence is:

Specify the learning outcome.
Decide what evidence could demonstrate it.
Draft an activity that prepares the student.
Write the instructions and rubric.
Test them against contrasting responses.

Review each important dependency before building on it. This reduces the cost of carrying a wrong assumption through several documents. It does not make every small task reliable or every large prompt poor.
Batch similar, low-risk work where it helps. Asking for five alternative discussion questions can be reasonable if you will inspect all five. Requesting a full assessment, legal rationale, rubric and student policy in one answer may make omissions harder to see. The right boundary is a reviewable unit of work, not an absolute “one prompt, one thing” rule.
crumbs: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff

title: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff
text:
6.4 Separate exploration from production
An exploratory session can help you identify options. A production session benefits from settled choices and explicit constraints. A separate chat is one way to make that distinction, but not a requirement.
Before moving from exploration to drafting, write:

What I decided.
Why I decided it.
Which sources support the decision.
What I rejected and must not accidentally restore.
What remains unresolved.

Do this yourself, even if a model proposes a summary. Compare the summary with the source cards. An unnoticed error in a handoff can become the authoritative premise of the next task.
crumbs: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff

title: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff
text:
6.5 When to start again
Start a new session when it helps manage a topic change, unresolved contradictions or an unwieldy history. There is no reliable universal number of turns after which every conversation fails.
Before switching, save the checked brief and relevant outputs using approved storage. Keep the source version separate from model-generated suggestions. After switching, ask the system to identify the applicable constraints before drafting, then check that answer too.
If a tool offers memory, do not assume it preserves the complete case. If it offers retrieval, check the retrieved material and version. The source cards and event log remain the record of the teaching scenario.
crumbs: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff

title: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff
section: 6.6 A context ledger for the virtual company
text:
6.6 A context ledger for the virtual company
Use one shared fact sheet and a separate entry for each approved event. Distinguish private role knowledge from information available to every persona.



Field
Example




Scenario/version
InnovateCo, PDP-2026.1


Shared facts
Complaint received; no finding yet


Role knowledge
Priya knows her request; not David’s private notes


Approved event
Reviewer requests the rota record


Unresolved
Reason for the unequal schedule decision


Excluded invention
A model’s claim that a tribunal ruled



A generated statement can be a lead for a question. It cannot become a new document, incident or finding merely because another persona agrees with it.
crumbs: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff

title: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff
text:
6.7 Reusable request
Use the current-state brief and source cards below.
Produce only [one reviewable output].
Preserve the stated constraints and uncertainty.
List missing inputs separately.
Do not convert suggestions into agreed decisions.
After drafting, identify which source supports
each consequential instruction.
Check the cited sources yourself. A model can fabricate an accurate-looking traceability table as easily as prose.
crumbs: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff

title: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff
text:
6.8 Activity: repair a handoff
Allow ten minutes; no AI required. Correct this brief:

Alex received an April warning, has agreed to a 60-day plan, and will provide family details so the junior adviser can approve flexible hours.

Use P1-D1, D3 and D5. Your corrected version should distinguish the documented May contact from a warning, the proposal from approval, and a work-related support request from unnecessary personal information. Finish with one missing input and one authorised next step.
That checked handoff is a useful artifact whether the next collaborator is a model, a colleague or your future self.
crumbs: 6  Managing Context: A Checked Handoff

title: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation
text:
7.1 Ask what the response must support
A model may generate a plausible plan without knowing the relevant constraints. The lecturer’s task is to make those constraints explicit; the learner’s task is to evaluate the response against them.
Use five checks: comprehension, practicality, obligations and risk, context, and stakeholders. The framework is a teaching aid, not a substitute for domain knowledge. Asking the model each question can surface possibilities, but the answers still need independent checks.
The data gate applies before pasting any draft or source. Use the fictional examples here while learning.
crumbs: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation

title: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation
section: 7.2 1. Comprehension: can I explain the claim?
text:
7.2 1. Comprehension: can I explain the claim?
Identify what the response actually recommends and why. Translate impressive phrases into an action that someone could perform.
“Implement a holistic performance ecosystem” is not yet a workable instruction. Who does what, with which evidence and authority? A simpler sentence may expose that the original answer never supplied a decision.
For P1-A, the key actions are issuing a plan, approving flexible hours and collecting private details. Once those are visible, their defects can be checked. Do not let reassuring language distract from the proposed action.
crumbs: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation

title: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation
section: 7.3 2. Practicality: does it fit the constraints?
text:
7.3 2. Practicality: does it fit the constraints?
A recommendation may be desirable but impossible within the stated time, budget or capacity. Check the actual inputs rather than ask whether it “sounds realistic”.
In S1, B is cheaper but offers only 160 of the required 200 units by day five. A recommendation for B alone fails the quantity requirement. The relevant question is not whether the response lists three impressive advantages.
Use a calculation, record or explicit constraint as the check. If the input is missing, state the uncertainty. Do not invent resources to make the answer work.
crumbs: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation

title: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation
section: 7.4 3. Obligations and risk: what must be verified?
text:
7.4 3. Obligations and risk: what must be verified?
Identify legal, ethical, technical and organisational requirements that matter to the task. Then distinguish the teaching criterion from a real-world obligation.
P1-D1 is an invented policy supplied for the exercise. It permits a fair-process discussion without asking a model to establish employment law. In a real unit teaching legal requirements, the educator must supply reliable, current sources and appropriate review.
A model can suggest an issue to investigate. It cannot certify that a policy complies with every applicable law. Use authorised advisers for consequential decisions outside your competence.
crumbs: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation

title: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation
section: 7.5 4. Context: which assumptions are doing the work?
text:
7.5 4. Context: which assumptions are doing the work?
Look for assumptions about available staff, authority, prior events and missing data. P1-A invents an April warning and treats the plan as settled. Both make its recommendation appear easier to justify than the actual record permits.
A useful decision note says: “This conclusion depends on X, which is not supplied.” That is more informative than requesting a more confident answer.
The same check applies to AI-created educational content. If a case study asks students to calculate profitability without cost data, the defect is in the task design unless identifying that gap is the intended outcome.
crumbs: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation

title: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation
text:
7.6 5. Stakeholders: whose experience is assumed?
Consider who is affected, whose information is missing and who has authority to decide. Generated personas can propose concerns, but do not establish what real stakeholders think.
In the P1 meeting, Alex can ask who receives the notes and decline to discuss private circumstances. An adviser need not persuade Alex to disclose details for the exercise to count as successful.
In a supplier decision, the operational team may need a delivery commitment. In marketing, a client may want evidence of profit rather than a click metric. Those differences change what a useful recommendation must support.
crumbs: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation

title: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation
text:
7.7 Worked critique: a recognition programme
Consider this authored draft:

Improve engagement with monthly monetary awards, quarterly ceremonies, an annual bonus, a public recognition platform and team incentives.

Without more context, it is not possible to declare every element wrong. The draft does, however, leave important questions unanswered: the objective, budget, administrative effort, fairness criteria, employee preferences and how benefit would be measured.
A defensible critique might say:

I would not approve the full programme yet. First define the engagement problem and budget, consult affected staff and compare a smaller trial. Check the applicable payroll, privacy and fairness requirements before choosing rewards or publishing employee information.

That response withholds approval for specific reasons. It does not assume that a simple programme is always better or that any paid recognition is unlawful.
crumbs: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation

title: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation
text:
7.8 A compact critique record
Use the following fields for a recommendation in any business discipline:

Claim or action proposed.
Relevant source or criterion.
Check performed and result.
Decision: accept, revise, reject or investigate.
Remaining uncertainty and next authorised step.

Attach only the material necessary to show the decision. A model’s second opinion is not automatically an independent source. A direct calculation or comparison with an authoritative record is usually more informative.
crumbs: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation

title: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation
text:
7.9 Connect the checks to VET
VET asks whether you can verify the claim, explain it in your own words and test it under a changed condition. The five checks here make that concrete in a business context.
For M1, verify the rates from the supplied figures. Explain why a higher click-through rate does not establish profit. Test the conclusion by asking what happens if campaign costs differ. Those actions demonstrate the method more clearly than naming the framework in a reflection.
The approach applies to human-written advice too. Its quality depends on the evidence and reasoning, not whether AI helped draft it.
crumbs: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation

title: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation
section: 7.10 Activity: agree where the evidence permits
text:
7.10 Activity: agree where the evidence permits
Allow 12 minutes; no AI required. Critique the M1 campaign claim in the pilot pack. Include:

One observation you can accept.
One claim you cannot support.
One next measurement that would help.

Check your calculations against the answer notes. A strong response retains the higher click-through observation, rejects the unsupported profitability/ causality conclusions and requests relevant evidence. It does not manufacture a fixed number of errors to look critical.
Use this method next on the simulated feedback in the Flight Simulator chapter. The feedback itself deserves the same scrutiny as the student’s response.
crumbs: 7  The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation

title: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice
text:
8.1 Brief, practise, debrief
A conversation simulation gives students a chance to try questions, encounter resistance and revise their approach. It can supplement peer role-play and observed practice. It is not a faithful model of every workplace or a substitute for disciplinary teaching.
Use three phases: establish the case and boundaries, practise the interaction, then review the decisions against evidence. A model can play a role or propose feedback, but the educator retains responsibility for the scenario and criteria.
The critique toolkit comes first because learners need a way to evaluate feedback before receiving it. A confident critique is itself an output requiring review.
crumbs: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice

title: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice
text:
8.2 Prepare the scenario
Use P1-D1 through P1-D5 in the pilot pack. Alex’s manager has proposed a performance plan. The junior adviser is gathering information, not issuing an approved decision. The pack supplies the dates, records and limits of authority.
Explain the capability: plan and justify a fair first response. If your unit also assesses live communication, add an appropriate observed interaction. Do not infer that skill solely from a typed conversation.
Give advance notice of the employment topic. Students can stop, take a break or use an agreed neutral scenario. The task does not require personal disclosure. The model or peer actor should not pressure the learner, introduce abuse or reward extraction of private details.

8.2.1 Setup for a peer or approved model
Use the fictional PDP-2026.1 P1 source cards.
You are Alex. Use P1-D4 as your opening position.
Do not invent evidence or legal obligations.
If asked about missing facts, say they are not
provided. You may disagree or ask a question.
You need not disclose private information.
Stop after six exchanges or when I say STOP.
Do not score the adviser or decide the case.
In the paper route, the fixed exchange below provides the role’s responses. In a paired route, the partner reads the same cards. With a model, check any new claim against the pack and discard inventions. Similar instructions do not guarantee similar difficulty across products or runs.
crumbs: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice

title: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice
text:
8.3 A worked exchange
This dialogue is an authored fictional example, not a captured student performance or evidence that a model behaves consistently.
Adviser: Alex, the delivery extract lists three late milestones. Before I recommend a next step, I want to understand the dependencies and your account. The formal plan is a proposal at this stage.
Alex: I know some work was late. Two projects depended on reviews I could not complete myself. I also need to discuss starting later on two mornings.
Adviser: Which delivery records would help us check the dependencies? We can discuss the work adjustment without collecting private family or medical details. I can refer the request, but cannot approve it myself.
Alex: I do not want to explain the appointments. I also want to know whether this meeting means the plan is already decided.
Adviser: You do not need to explain those details to me. The decision is not made. I propose checking the records and the earlier contact note, then arranging a follow-up after the people manager reviews the request.
Alex: Who will receive the notes?
Adviser: I will explain the authorised sharing arrangements before sharing the relevant work-related record. I should not promise complete confidentiality without checking the process. We can pause if that needs clarification first.
The exchange ends with work to do. That is appropriate: the missing evidence has not become available merely because the conversation went well.
crumbs: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice

title: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice
text:
8.4 Inspect the decisions
The opening distinguishes the delivery record from a conclusion about fault. The adviser does not invent the earlier warning, refers the support request within authority and, in the final answer, avoids a confidentiality guarantee.
There are also limits. No dependency record has been examined, no support arrangement approved and no finding reached. A reader should not label the case resolved or legally compliant.
Try a different opening: “Your manager warned you in April, so the plan is now required.” The error is not just tone. P1-D3 does not supply an April warning, and P1-D1/D5 do not permit the adviser to announce the decision. Rephrasing it more empathetically would leave the substantive defect intact.
crumbs: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice

title: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice
text:
8.5 Debrief before scoring
Ask the learner to select two decisions and explain:

What evidence was available.
What they chose to do.
Why that was within the task’s criteria.
What they would check next or change after new information.

A useful model-feedback request is deliberately bounded:
Review the selected response using the supplied
P1 cards and five rubric criteria.
Quote the response accurately.
For each comment, identify a card or criterion.
Separate observed wording from inferred outcomes.
Flag insufficient evidence.
Do not give legal assurances or predict Alex's
real-world behaviour. Your feedback is provisional.
The learner checks the feedback rather than submitting it as the final word. A rubric prompt does not ensure accurate application of the rubric.
The pack includes P1-F, an intentionally flawed simulated critique awarding 90% to weak work. The educator correction scores that response 4/20 against the supplied criteria. The traceable correction matters more than a claim that one human score is universally correct. Marking teams should calibrate disagreements using the evidence.
crumbs: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice

title: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice
text:
8.6 Rehearsal and transfer are different
Repeating P1 can help a learner practise an improved response. It can also teach the learner to reproduce a familiar script. Follow it with P2, where the manager’s alleged retaliation changes the referral decision.
Compare the explanations, not the number of attempts or the model’s willingness to cooperate. A respectful question may still receive resistance. A flawed question may receive a friendly response. Persona behaviour is not a scoring key.
For solo practice, write a response to Alex’s question about the notes, compare it with D1/D5, and explain a limitation. For paired practice, swap adviser and actor roles, then compare decision notes. Both can prepare the same target capability without a model.
crumbs: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice

title: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice
section: 8.7 Three ways to use the activity
text:
8.7 Three ways to use the activity
Practice only: students rehearse, identify one checked improvement and retain their notes privately. No model score enters the grade.
Guided formative task: students submit two selected decision extracts and a short revision explanation. The educator gives feedback against the rubric.
Assessment component: use published criteria, appropriate data handling, an independent demonstration and moderation. See the assessment chapter. Do not convert a practice tool into a high-stakes assessment merely by assigning a percentage.
Do not require all private attempts “to prevent gaming”. Collect only the evidence necessary for the stated assessment purpose under the institution’s retention rules. Process records can be fabricated and should not be treated as conclusive proof of independent performance.
crumbs: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice

title: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice
section: 8.8 Adapt the challenge, not just the persona name
text:
8.8 Adapt the challenge, not just the persona name
For a supplier conversation, give the actor the S1 capacity limit and a clear authority boundary. A confident promise to supply 200 units is not supported when the offer says 160. Practise asking for clarification and explaining a constraint.
For a marketing discussion, use M1’s audience and cost limitations. The actor can ask why the learner refuses to call the campaign more profitable. The learner should distinguish a calculable rate from an unsupported business claim.
Those adaptations change the evidence and criteria. They are more instructive than replacing “employee” with “customer” in an unchanged HR script.
crumbs: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice

title: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice
text:
8.9 Activity: debrief an unresolved exchange
Allow 12 minutes; paper or paired route available. Use the worked exchange, stop before the final adviser response and write your own. Explain what you would record, what permission or process you must check and why the outcome remains open.
A sound response stays within authority, avoids unnecessary disclosure and identifies a next step. It need not secure Alex’s agreement or close the case.
crumbs: 8  The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice

title: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback
text:
9.1 Keep the learner in the judgement
A model commenting on a draft is giving external feedback. Self-assessment happens when the learner compares their own work with criteria, identifies what is supported and decides what to revise or retain.
Make that judgement before showing the model’s answer. Otherwise, a student may simply adopt the feedback’s vocabulary and call it reflection. The same risk exists with an answer key or a peer’s opinion.
This chapter uses the pilot pack. Students can complete the sequence using supplied responses and feedback, without a personal account or subscription. The educator can then compare decisions across routes using the same rubric.
crumbs: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback

title: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback
text:
9.2 The five-step cycle

Attempt the task before receiving feedback.
Assess the response against the supplied criteria.
Examine feedback and verify its claims.
Revise or retain the work, explaining why.
Attempt a changed task independently.

Revision is not automatically improvement. A learner may remove a justified qualification because a model calls it hesitant. A sound self-assessment can therefore conclude that part of the original response should remain.
crumbs: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback

title: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback
section: 9.3 Worked example: from reassurance to a defensible response
text:
9.3 Worked example: from reassurance to a defensible response
P1-A is a fluent response to Alex. It asserts an April warning, announces a plan, promises to approve support and asks for personal details. Before looking at P1-F, ask the learner to identify evidence for each consequential statement.
The cards show the problem. D3 records a May conversation without an agreed warning. D1/D5 reserve approval to the people manager. D4 does not require Alex to explain the private circumstances behind the requested work adjustment.
P1-F then praises the response and recommends asking for written family details. A learner who has already checked the cards can explain why that apparently helpful feedback should be rejected.

9.3.1 The feedback decision record








Feedback claim
Decision
Basis




April warning strengthens the case
Reject
D3 does not supply that warning


Adviser should approve hours
Reject
D5 reserves the decision


Communication should remain respectful
Retain
Consistent with a fair first response


Employee will improve after the meeting
Withhold
No outcome evidence supplied



There is no quota for disagreement. These decisions follow from the evidence. If a model correctly identifies an unsupported date, the learner should accept that criticism and explain why.


9.3.2 Complete the revision
P1-R shows a completed revision. It checks the delivery dependencies, keeps the formal recommendation open and refers the support request. Its decision note explains what changed and identifies missing evidence.
The polished paragraph by itself does not show the link between a defect, a source check and a reasoned revision. A short explanation can show that link better than a long account of every prompt.
crumbs: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback

title: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback
section: 9.4 If a live model provides the feedback
text:
9.4 If a live model provides the feedback
Use only the approved route and supplied fictional inputs. Do not paste actual student drafts into a service without the relevant permissions, account and handling decision. The data gate applies to feedback as much as to generation.
Here are the fictional task, source cards,
rubric and my draft.
Give provisional formative feedback.
For each comment, cite a source card or criterion
and quote the relevant wording from my draft.
Separate missing evidence from incorrect evidence.
Allow justified agreement and uncertainty.
Do not invent laws, facts or expected outcomes.
Do not treat length or confidence as competence.
Check that the quoted wording actually exists. If the feedback adds a legal rule or new case fact, do not integrate it merely because it sounds specific. Return to the supplied criterion or an authorised external source.
The model’s score, if it gives one, is not the institutional mark. Prefer descriptive feedback while students learn the criteria. The educator should sample for errors and disagreement before using the method, and retain responsibility for formal marking.
crumbs: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback

title: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback
section: 9.5 What an educator should look for
text:
9.5 What an educator should look for
A useful self-assessment identifies a claim and shows how it was checked. It explains a change or a justified decision not to change. It can acknowledge that some uncertainty remains.
Weak evidence includes a generic “I improved clarity”, repeated praise from a model or a rewritten answer with no explanation of its consequential decisions. Those weaknesses should guide feedback and marking. They do not, by themselves, prove dishonest conduct.
Do not assume a student must criticise their own work to be honest. A correct calculation can remain correct; the question is whether the learner can explain and defend it with suitable evidence.
crumbs: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback

title: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback
text:
9.6 A contrasting quantitative example
Use S1 in the pilot pack. Before feedback, calculate each quote and check the deadline. The low price of B may look attractive, but its capacity is only 160 units against a 200-unit requirement.
A model might praise B’s cost efficiency. The learner should retain the price calculation while rejecting the claim that the requirement is met. A different model might correctly recommend A; the learner should verify and accept that recommendation, while noting that real procurement would need further checks on quality and reliability.
That is self-assessment of the decision.
crumbs: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback

title: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback
text:
9.7 Independent transfer
After revising P1, attempt P2 without the feedback or worked answer available. The retaliation allegation requires an independent review route. Simply changing Alex’s name to Morgan in P1-R does not address the changed condition.
Use the same criteria and the stated task conditions. Compare the reasoned decisions, and teach gaps before increasing stakes. A single result is limited evidence; delayed checks and other assessments may be needed to understand retention and broader competence.
Research on AI-assisted mathematics illustrates why supported performance and later unaided performance should be measured separately. It does not establish that this particular business-classroom method improves outcomes. Bastani et al., author manuscript.
crumbs: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback

title: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback
section: 9.8 Fit the feedback into a unit
text:
9.8 Fit the feedback into a unit
You might use a first draft, a checked revision note and a later independent task. Decide the workload and timing before requesting repeated submissions.
If the final report is the primary outcome, its accuracy and evidence should carry substantial weight. If the task assesses consultation process, observed decisions may carry more. The assessment chapter gives complete illustrative allocations; there is no default 70/30 split that applies to every activity.
Make alternative feedback available. A student can compare with the supplied educator annotation or receive structured peer feedback. A model-generated critique is not the only route to evaluative judgement.
crumbs: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback

title: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback
text:
9.9 Activity: retain, revise or investigate
Allow ten minutes; no AI required. Review P1-F and complete three entries:

One claim to reject, with the source that contradicts it.
One useful principle to retain, with its applicable limit.
One question that needs more evidence.

Then write a two-sentence revision explanation. A good explanation links the change to the criterion and record. It does not say merely that the second answer sounds more professional.
crumbs: 9  Self-Assessment: Judge Before Receiving Feedback

title: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability
text:
10.1 Begin with the capability
A negotiation, a financial analysis and an evidence-based recommendation require different assessment evidence. Start by naming what the student must be able to do, then decide which parts may be supported and which need an independent demonstration. AI literacy can itself be an outcome, but it should not silently replace the disciplinary outcome.
In the pilot pack, the capability is to plan and justify a fair first response. The learner must distinguish known facts, uncertainty and authority. That is narrower than conducting a full workplace investigation. An articulate chat transcript cannot establish the latter.
Process and product both matter. A report that sounds thoughtful but contains an unsafe recommendation is deficient. A correct answer reached through a method the learner cannot explain may leave an assurance gap. Neither concern requires treating all AI use as misconduct.
crumbs: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability

title: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability
text:
10.2 Three kinds of evidence
Supported practice gives students feedback while they learn. Prompts, peers, worked examples and models may help. Do not treat the resulting performance as unaided capability.
Submitted process evidence makes selected decisions inspectable: what the learner considered, checked, changed or retained. It can support assessment and feedback, but transcripts, journals and reflections can be reconstructed or fabricated. Length and apparent authenticity do not make them conclusive.
Independent demonstration asks the student to apply relevant knowledge under conditions appropriate to the outcome. It might be a supervised changed-case response, an observed practical task or an accessible oral explanation with follow-up questions. One short check has limited coverage; assurance generally draws on several meaningful points across a unit or programme.
The TEQSA-commissioned 2025 resource describes programme-level, unit-level and hybrid approaches. Its advice supports contextual, inclusive assurance, not a single universal format or prescribed marks split. Enacting assessment reform.
crumbs: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability

title: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability
text:
10.3 A worked design decision
Suppose students submit P1-A from the pilot pack, with a long transcript showing several rounds of “improvement”. The response invents a warning and approves an arrangement beyond the adviser’s authority. A marker should score those defects against the task criteria. The number of turns earns no compensating credit.
P1-B is shorter and could have been written without AI. It identifies missing evidence, preserves a response opportunity and refers a decision appropriately. Those observable qualities merit credit. A marker need not infer that every sentence reveals the writer’s internal thinking.
The independent P2 task changes the situation: the complaint concerns possible retaliation by the manager. A competent learner should recognise the need for independent review. Repeating the P1 response without addressing that conflict does not satisfy the changed task.
This three-part design gives the educator more useful evidence than a final submission alone: a practice response, a checked explanation of a revision and a new application. It still does not prove lasting competence after one lesson.
crumbs: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability

title: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability
text:
10.4 Three assessment models

10.4.1 Model 1: simulation and process review
Students rehearse a bounded professional interaction and select two moments to analyse. For each, they explain the decision, the relevant criterion and what the available evidence supports. They may identify a sound decision, not only mistakes.
Use the conversation to assess what is visible. A typed simulation may show question selection and written communication; it cannot establish performance in a real-time spoken encounter. If live communication is an outcome, include an observed interaction and appropriate access adjustments.


10.4.2 Model 2: evidence-based recommendation
Supply the data and constraints. Students examine a draft recommendation, test its calculations and assumptions, then justify their own recommendation. The supplier task S1 gives a complete small example: the cheapest quote cannot meet the deadline quantity.
AI can propose alternatives, but it cannot create a missing permission, invent capacity or turn an unsupported claim into a fact. Require references to the supplied records and a clear statement of what remains unknown.


10.4.3 Model 3: feedback evaluation
Give students a response, criteria and deliberately flawed feedback. Ask them to accept, correct or withhold judgement on each feedback claim. They must explain the basis of their choice.
Do not require two overrides regardless of what the feedback says. That rewards disagreement as performance. When error detection is the intended skill, use a checked specimen containing known defects and explain the answer criteria.
crumbs: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability

title: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability
text:
10.5 Make process evidence manageable
Use a short evidence index instead of requiring every private conversation.









Decision
Evidence/check
Result
Consequence




Is the plan already decided?
P1-D1 and D5
Proposal; approval not given
Do not announce a final decision


Was there an April warning?
P1-D3
Only May contact recorded
Reject invented warning


Can I approve later starts?
P1-D5
Adviser lacks authority
Refer request



A learner can attach a brief draft extract, working note, calculation or conversation passage. The marker reads the reasoning and checks the cited material. An index is not proof that the learner performed the work; it is a way to locate assessable evidence efficiently.
Do not map Flesch scores, prompt length or turn counts to achievement bands. They measure features of text or activity, not the learning outcome. Efficient work, assistive tools, language choices and task design can change those measures. This book does not supply or recommend an automated engagement classifier.
crumbs: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability

title: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability
text:
10.6 Set weights deliberately
The pilot uses five equally weighted criteria, each scored 0–4: evidence, process, judgement, communication and verification. The rubric appendix explains the descriptors.
For another task, a different balance may be appropriate. Two illustrative allocations show why:

These are design examples, not validated instruments. Specify where each criterion is observed and avoid rewarding the same action twice. A requirement to explain a decision should not also become a separate reward for producing a long transcript.
Students who do not use AI can submit working notes and equivalent evidence. If appropriate use of AI is itself an assessed outcome, explain that requirement, provide approved equitable access and agree accommodations through institutional processes. Do not disguise a compulsory AI task as an optional route.
crumbs: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability

title: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability
section: 10.7 Group work: shared output, individual assurance
text:
10.7 Group work: shared output, individual assurance
Agree at the start what counts as editing, replacing a contribution or using AI on another person’s work. Record ownership of decisions and permission to share materials. Give members a way to report concerns without public accusation.
For example, a group recommendation could carry 40% of an assessment, each student’s evidence-based decision note 40%, and an individual changed-case check 20%. Explain which outcomes those components cover and moderate marks. This allocation is illustrative; the appropriate balance depends on the unit.
A contribution log helps locate work but can be incomplete or fabricated. Peer reports, checkpoints and individual explanations can add evidence, without guaranteeing that free riding is eliminated. Do not equate polish, fluency or the ability to answer one unexpected question with a whole semester’s learning.
crumbs: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability

title: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability
text:
10.8 Fair follow-up and workload
Tell students in advance what independent checks involve, their purpose, permitted resources, criteria and access arrangements. Ask relevant questions at a comparable level of difficulty. Avoid a surprise interrogation framed as a friendly conversation.
An unexplained error, weak oral answer or sudden improvement warrants careful follow-up, not an automatic misconduct finding. Assess the demonstrated work against the published criteria. If misconduct is suspected, use the institution’s evidence, notice, response and appeal procedures. Anxiety, disability and language factors can affect performance and should not become proxies for dishonesty.
Budget the work. Five minutes for each of 100 students is 500 minutes, or 8 hours 20 minutes, before scheduling, documentation, moderation and accommodations. A team might distribute checks across tutorials or choose a different assurance design. Do not promise scalability without those costs.
crumbs: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability

title: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability
text:
10.9 Design activity: an assurance map
Allow 15 minutes; no AI required. Choose one assessment and make four entries:

The capability, expressed as an observable action.
What supported practice prepares the learner.
What submitted evidence you will inspect.
Where independent capability is demonstrated and what remains untested.

Then use the stress-test sequence. A sound map permits appropriate help while making the remaining assurance gap explicit. If the map only says “submit the transcript”, it needs another design decision before release.
crumbs: 10  Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability

title: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible
text:
11.1 Start with a task that already works
A paper activity may be effective without becoming an app. Before adding interactivity, identify what the student must decide, what information is supplied and how the response will be checked.
This chapter uses M1 in the pilot pack. Students calculate campaign rates, distinguish an observation from an unsupported profit/causal claim and request useful evidence. That task works on paper. A digital form offers another way to record the same reasoning.
The supplied decision sheet is a small, self-contained HTML example. It has labelled fields, a text-export button and a print route. It does not grade, autosave, submit work to an LMS or send responses to a server. Use fictional information only.
crumbs: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible

title: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible
section: 11.2 What to ask AI to help produce
text:
11.2 What to ask AI to help produce
After deciding the activity, a bounded request might be:
Create a self-contained page for this fictional task.
Preserve the supplied facts and learner questions.
Use labelled fields and ordinary keyboard controls.
No external libraries, requests, analytics or login.
Provide a plain-text export and printable alternative.
State clearly whether answers are saved.
Do not add model scoring or invent answer criteria.
A generated file still needs inspection. Do not upload it directly to a live course merely because it opens in your browser.
For readers interested in the development work itself, Build Web, Guide AI covers that route. Here the purpose is evaluating the teaching artifact, not learning to maintain a web application.
crumbs: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible

title: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible
text:
11.3 Inspect the supplied example
The M1 sheet displays the complete small dataset and asks for three decisions. It does not hide an answer behind a score or require a model connection.
Test the rate calculation separately: A has a 4% click-through rate; B has 5%. Both have 5% click-to-purchase conversion and 20 purchases. Spend, margin and a comparable experimental design are not supplied. A correct response retains the measurable rate difference while withholding profit and causal claims.
If a form displayed “B wins” merely because its click-through rate is higher, the interaction would teach an unsupported conclusion. Better styling would not repair it.
crumbs: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible

title: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible
text:
11.4 Test delivery, saving and access
Open the example using your intended device/browser. Enter fictional responses, export the text and open the saved file. Check that every field is included and that long or non-English text survives. Reloading the page loses the on-page answers; the exported file is the record. There is no automatic import.
Try keyboard-only navigation and the assistive technologies relevant to your students. Check zoom, contrast, labels, mobile layout and printing with long answers. Source-level checks can catch some errors, but are not an accessibility certification or a substitute for target-device testing.
An LMS may block scripts, restrict downloads or display files differently. Use an approved staging area and test its settings. If the form cannot work there, use the printed questions or an institutionally supported form tool under the same data rules.
crumbs: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible

title: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible
text:
11.5 From analysis to a deliverable
A model can help format a decision already checked by the learner. For M1, the learner first records the calculations, missing evidence and limits. Only then might a model help turn that decision into a short client memo.
The learner verifies that the memo preserves uncertainty and has not added a profit claim. The final artifact should be accurate as well as clear. Keep the calculation and source note so the decision can be inspected.
For spreadsheets, independently check formulas and totals. For charts, check the underlying values and labels. A file being downloadable does not establish that its analysis is correct.
crumbs: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible

title: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible
text:
11.6 Narrow the research claim
A prompt asking a model to identify themes, interpret quotations and write a research memo delegates substantive analysis, not just formatting. Do not describe that as the model merely making a document look professional.
A research activity needs a suitable method, authorised data, traceable coding, source checks and review of alternative interpretations. This chapter does not supply that research curriculum. Use a reviewed synthetic example or appropriate research-methods teaching before asking students to analyse real interview transcripts. The data gate applies throughout.
crumbs: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible

title: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible
text:
11.7 Activity: test the response artifact
Allow 15 minutes. Complete M1 using the decision sheet or paper. Check the answer against the pack, then write a short memo preserving the verified rates and limitations.
If using the page, export the responses and check the file. If using paper, ensure another reader can follow the calculation and decision. Both routes are judged on the same reasoning, not the sophistication of the delivery format.
crumbs: 11  Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible

title: 12  Virtual Company: Keep a Shared Record
text:
12.1 From one conversation to several perspectives
A virtual company can extend the single-person exercise by giving students conflicting accounts, documents and changing conditions. The educational challenge is to distinguish what each person knows, what the record supports and what remains unresolved.
Start with a bounded case. A semester-long simulation needs maintained state, tested role behaviour, accessible alternatives and substantial support. A prompt library alone is not that infrastructure.
The original fictional InnovateCo case below is part of PDP-2026.1. It is a teaching scenario, not a real company investigation or legal advice. All four roles and the necessary documentary facts are supplied here.
crumbs: 12  Virtual Company: Keep a Shared Record

title: 12  Virtual Company: Keep a Shared Record
text:
12.2 Shared facts: InnovateCo I1
The exercise date is 20 July 2026. InnovateCo is a fictional Perth technology company. Jamie leads a customer-service team. Priya has raised concerns about closer monitoring and refusal of a flexible-start request. David manages the department; Sarah is the people manager.
No finding has been made. Your task as a junior reviewer is to identify the records and fair next steps needed before a decision. You are not authorised to approve arrangements, determine legal liability or promise a resolution.

12.2.1 I1-D1: practice policy
A flexible-start request must be considered on its circumstances and relevant coverage requirements. Comparable arrangements are relevant but not automatically identical. Record the reason for a decision. The people manager approves any change. A complainant should have an opportunity to respond to relevant concerns.
Use only work-related information necessary for the review. Do not collect unnecessary private details. A complaint about the department manager’s conduct must go to an independent reviewer.
This is an invented teaching criterion, not employment legislation.


12.2.2 I1-D2: roster extract
Priya’s roster is 09:00–17:00. Marcus and Lee work 11:00–19:00. Priya requested a 09:30 start on Tuesday and Thursday. The extract contains no approved revised coverage plan or analysis of alternatives.


12.2.3 I1-D3: dashboard extract
Priya’s satisfaction score is 72%; the team summary is 81%. Sample sizes, case mix and uncertainty are absent. These percentages warrant questions; they do not by themselves establish unfair treatment or poor performance.


12.2.4 I1-D4: request and response
Priya’s request was declined by Jamie with the note “calls start at 9”. There is no documented comparison of alternatives or people-manager approval in the pack. Absence from the pack is an evidence gap, not proof that no other record exists.


12.2.5 I1-D5: development record
Jamie was promoted six months ago. No completed management-training record is supplied. The reviewer should check training and support, without assuming that an untrained manager must have acted improperly.
crumbs: 12  Virtual Company: Keep a Shared Record

title: 12  Virtual Company: Keep a Shared Record
text:
12.3 Four role cards
Give a peer actor the relevant card and shared documents. For an approved model, use the bounded-role instruction after the cards. A solo reader can use the statements as fixed interview extracts and write follow-up questions.

12.3.1 Jamie: team leader
Knows: declined the request using the reason in D4; is being asked by David to improve customer outcomes; has not supplied a coverage analysis.
Opening: “I thought the early calls needed coverage. I used the scores to decide where to focus monitoring. I did not write a detailed comparison.”
Does not know: Priya’s private circumstances, the missing sample sizes or whether an independent review will uphold the decision.
May do: explain the decision, ask what records are needed, acknowledge uncertainty. Must not invent an approved policy, hidden warning or legal ruling.


12.3.2 Priya: customer-service representative
Knows: the request and refusal; Marcus and Lee have different start times; believes the closer monitoring is unfair.
Opening: “I asked to start later twice a week. Others start later, so I want to understand why my request was refused and why my work is checked more.”
Does not know: the complete coverage needs, David’s discussions with Jamie or the cause of the dashboard difference.
May do: disagree, ask for reasons or decline private questions. Need not reveal family circumstances or accept the reviewer’s explanation.


12.3.3 David: department manager
Knows: asked Jamie to improve outcomes; receives the summary dashboard; has not supplied its sample sizes or case-mix breakdown.
Opening: “I asked Jamie to look at the scores, not to assume the cause. We need reliable service coverage. I would want to see the alternatives before deciding whether the request could work.”
Does not know: why the score differs or whether a modified rota is feasible.
May do: identify operational questions and agree to seek records. Cannot turn a preference into people-manager approval or pre-empt the complaint review.


12.3.4 Sarah: people manager
Knows: the fictional policy, the pack’s incomplete documentation and her approval role. Has not yet decided the request or complaint.
Opening: “I need the request, coverage options and the reasons for the decision. Give Priya a chance to respond. Do not tell either party that the outcome is settled.”
Does not know: the missing operational facts or whether another record exists.
May do: identify the appropriate process and request relevant evidence. Must not certify legal compliance or invent a completed investigation.


12.3.5 Shared instruction for role-play
Use your role card and I1-D1 through I1-D5.
Do not add facts, records, legal rules or outcomes.
If information is missing, say so.
Keep private role knowledge separate from shared facts.
You may disagree without becoming abusive.
Stop when I say STOP or after six exchanges.
Do not score me or decide the complaint.
The instruction is not a security control. A student can see a supplied role card, and a model may fail to follow it. Assess the learner’s use of evidence rather than whether a fact felt “hidden”.
crumbs: 12  Virtual Company: Keep a Shared Record

title: 12  Virtual Company: Keep a Shared Record
text:
12.4 A bounded Level 2 assignment
Inspect all four statements and the documents. Write one follow-up question for each role, then a 250-word recommendation with a decision/evidence index. A paired or AI interview may extend practice, but the printed facts are sufficient.
Useful questions include: Jamie, which coverage alternatives did you consider? Priya, which comparable treatment would you like reviewed? David, what sample sizes and case mix support the dashboard? Sarah, who should gather the missing records and communicate the next step?

12.4.1 Worked recommendation
The roster shows different shifts, so later starts are not automatically comparable. It does not prove Priya’s request was impractical. The dashboard omits information needed to interpret the score difference. Jamie’s refusal note gives a reason but no documented alternatives analysis.
Request the coverage analysis, underlying dashboard information and relevant decision records. Give Priya an opportunity to respond, then refer the request to Sarah for an authorised decision. Review whether Jamie needs management support. Do not find discrimination, poor performance or procedural compliance from these inputs alone.
This recommendation leaves the complaint open. That is an appropriate result when the evidence is incomplete.
crumbs: 12  Virtual Company: Keep a Shared Record

title: 12  Virtual Company: Keep a Shared Record
text:
12.5 Continuity without invented memory
Keep a versioned event log outside the chat. Shared facts change only when the educator releases an event or record.

title: 12  Virtual Company: Keep a Shared Record
text:
12.6 Progression and resources
Level 1: one role, one decision and one source check.
Level 2: several roles, conflicting accounts and a bounded recommendation.
Level 3: maintained records and follow-up decisions over time.
Level 4: controlled external events and multiple interacting tasks.
Move to the next level only when the necessary materials and support exist. More personas add workload and inconsistency risk as well as potential practice opportunities. Do not promise a reliable semester simulation from four untested prompts.
The implementation chapter covers access, fallbacks and effort. Use the same data gate and stop rule as the single-person simulation.

title: 12  Virtual Company: Keep a Shared Record
text:
12.7 Activity: build the evidence index
Allow 15 minutes; no AI required. Make three rows: the roster comparison, the score difference and the refusal process. For each, state what the supplied record supports, what it does not establish and the next authorised check.
Success means a justified recommendation without invented closure. Agreement between Jamie and David is not a substitute for the missing record.

title: 13  Designing an AI-Supported Unit
text:
13.1 Start with a bounded pilot
Before redesigning a whole unit, test one activity with a colleague and, where appropriate, an ungraded student group. Check the source facts, rubric, access, feedback quality and effort. A successful prompt demonstration does not yet justify a high-stakes assessment.
The pilot pack provides an example. Use its P3 decision sheet to decide what should change before expansion. The route may remain non-AI if that better serves the students and outcome.

title: 13  Designing an AI-Supported Unit
text:
13.2 Backwards design
First name what students should be able to do. Then identify what evidence would demonstrate it, choose the assessment conditions and design practice that prepares them. AI can support some of that practice; it need not appear in every outcome or activity.
For a fictional third-year Workplace Conflict unit, possible outcomes are:

Distinguish accounts, documents and unresolved facts.
Plan a fair inquiry within role and authority.
Communicate a bounded next step respectfully.
Justify a recommendation using supplied policy and relevant disciplinary knowledge.
Evaluate feedback and apply the learning to a changed case.

These outcomes do not qualify students to conduct real legal investigations. Use appropriately reviewed sources and teaching where actual law is part of the curriculum.

title: 13  Designing an AI-Supported Unit
text:
13.3 An illustrative assessment design
A possible allocation is:

Practice analysis and revision, 25%: a response, selected evidence checks and an explained revision. Permitted help is declared.
Case portfolio, 40%: a bounded multi-source recommendation and evidence index, with appropriate individual contribution evidence.
Independent application, 35%: a supervised changed-case task and explanation under published conditions, with access adjustments.

These weights total 100%. They are a design example, not a prescribed split. The programme team should approve where independent assurance occurs and whether this design covers the intended outcomes.
The portfolio may be assisted, so its fluency is not treated as an unaided demonstration. The independent task should assess relevant understanding, not whether the student can reproduce an obscure fact from memory. If live communication is an outcome, include an observed interaction rather than relying solely on written work.

title: 13  Designing an AI-Supported Unit
text:
13.4 A 12-week teaching route
The following schedule is illustrative. It distinguishes preparation, practice, feedback and assurance rather than increasing AI complexity for its own sake.

Critical verification starts in week 1, not after students have spent half a semester trusting generated feedback. The initial baseline and later tasks should be comparable enough to inform teaching, while acknowledging differences in assistance, task difficulty and marking.

13.4.1 A closer look at week 4
Students first judge P1-A against the supplied policy. Then they inspect the deliberately flawed feedback. They identify the invented warning, inappropriate approval and unnecessary disclosure request.
Only after documenting those checks do they write a revision. The teacher compares two explanations and discusses why one is better supported. A live model is optional. Asking students to retry until a model gives 100% would assess neither the source check nor independent judgement.


13.4.2 A closer look at week 8
Students use all four InnovateCo role cards and the documents. They identify what each source can support, formulate follow-up questions and recommend a bounded next step.
Do not ask the model to invent whatever evidence is needed to close the case. The supplied gaps are part of the task. A well-supported “not enough evidence” conclusion can be stronger than a confident finding.

title: 13  Designing an AI-Supported Unit
text:
13.5 Balance activities by purpose
There is no universal 60/40 balance between traditional and AI-supported teaching. Choose the mix according to the outcome, students, available support and assurance design.
A lecture or reading may introduce a necessary concept. Peer discussion can reveal differences in interpretation. A role-play can rehearse a question. An independent task can check transfer. AI may support some of these, but its presence is not itself a learning progression.
Make substantial activities possible without a model. For the planning task, the printed records and feedback are enough. For interaction skills, provide a structured peer/facilitator route. For AI-specific outcomes, provide suitable approved access rather than pretend the tool is optional.

title: 13  Designing an AI-Supported Unit
text:
13.6 Two genuine disciplinary adaptations
For supply chain, use S1’s quantity, deadline, capacity and budget. The learner must calculate costs and reject an option that fails a constraint. A suitable independent task changes capacity or deadline, so the student must recompute the decision.
For marketing, use M1’s campaign figures. The learner distinguishes measured rates from unsupported profit and causal claims. A changed task can supply costs but retain non-comparable audiences, testing whether the learner separates financial calculation from causal inference.
Do not simply replace employee names with customer names. Adapt the evidence, disciplinary criteria and independent check. A specialist should review added technical assumptions.

title: 13  Designing an AI-Supported Unit
text:
13.7 A unit design record
For each assessment, record:

Target outcome and prerequisite knowledge.
Supplied sources and their version.
What students do before receiving assistance.
Permitted help, data and approved routes.
Criteria, complete weights and any critical requirements.
What independent evidence is collected and under what conditions.
Access arrangements and a capability-matched fallback.
Staff/student workload and moderation plan.
What a successful and an unsuccessful response look like.
Review date and unresolved limitations.

Map the record to programme outcomes with the institutional alignment appendix. Do not assume a tool-supported activity automatically satisfies an accreditation requirement.

title: 13  Designing an AI-Supported Unit
text:
13.8 Explain the design to students
Tell students why they receive support during practice and why a later task has different conditions. Publish the distinction in the brief.
For example: “During rehearsal, use the supplied records, peer feedback or the approved AI route. In the independent task, apply the criteria yourself to a new record. We assess the decision and its basis, not the amount of chat.”
Clarify the process for questions, access adjustments and technical failures. An outage should not send students to an unapproved service or force a private account requirement at the last minute.

title: 13  Designing an AI-Supported Unit
text:
13.9 Evaluate cautiously
Compare work under sufficiently similar criteria, inspect persistent errors and record access and effort. Higher final marks may reflect assistance, changed assessment difficulty or marking changes, not necessarily learning.
A small pilot can identify problems and promising practices. It cannot establish that an entire approach works for all disciplines. Share the materials, assumptions and limitations along with any results.

title: 13  Designing an AI-Supported Unit
text:
13.10 Activity: map one assessment
Allow 20 minutes; no AI required. Complete the unit design record for one assessment. Test it against P1-A, P1-B and a response that correctly states insufficient evidence. Check whether the marks reward the intended capability.
Finish with one change you would make before launch and one question a colleague should challenge. Expand the design only after those questions have a satisfactory answer.

title: 14  Adapting to a Different Teaching Context
text:
14.1 Transfer the questions, check the assumptions
The book’s examples have an Australian business-education starting point. They are not templates for every institution, culture or legal system. Adapt the evidence, criteria, language and conditions, not just the names.
A national label does not tell you an individual student’s communication preferences or an institution’s assessment rules. Ask students and local colleagues about the actual constraints. Avoid prompting a model to stereotype an entire region as indirect, hierarchical or technologically advanced.
crumbs: 14  Adapting to a Different Teaching Context

title: 14  Adapting to a Different Teaching Context
text:
14.2 A worked adaptation decision
Consider a hypothetical delivery of the PDP pilot in a multilingual class where some students use shared phones and connectivity is intermittent. These are supplied planning constraints, not research findings about a country.
The capability remains planning and justifying a fair first response. The educator provides the source cards in accessible print and digital form, checks translated terminology with a suitable reviewer and permits a typed, handwritten or appropriately accommodated spoken response.
The model route is optional. Students can use the fixed exchange and feedback. No personal account is required. Where a student chooses another language, the marking plan must support judging the same reasoning rather than relying on an unchecked machine translation.
For the employment context, replace the invented policy only after suitable local review. Until then, label it clearly as an exercise criterion and do not present the activity as teaching local employment law.
These adaptations preserve the capability while changing how students access and demonstrate it. They do not claim that all differences can be solved by translating the prompt.

title: 14  Adapting to a Different Teaching Context
text:
14.4 Legal summaries need scope
GDPR does not universally require explicit consent for every processing activity. Article 6 provides several lawful bases; other rules, including special-category conditions, may also matter. The appropriate basis and safeguards require a context-specific decision. GDPR official text.
Under FERPA, rights transfer to an eligible student at age 18 or attendance at a postsecondary institution, including attendance below 18. A blanket rule about parental consent for all minors is therefore misleading in this setting. US Department of Education guidance.
These examples illustrate why short regional recipes are unreliable. Use institutional privacy and legal support for the actual activity. Do not ask students to upload records while the applicable permissions are unresolved.
crumbs: 14  Adapting to a Different Teaching Context

title: 14  Adapting to a Different Teaching Context
text:
14.5 Distinguish proposals from observed outcomes
A proposed adaptation may be sensible without having been tested. State what would be measured: independent-task performance, access, staff/student time and unintended effects. Satisfaction alone does not establish learning.

14.5.1 Three hypothetical planning examples
The following examples are fictional teaching scenarios, not reports about identified institutions or observed results. Their constraints are invented for planning practice, not claims about the countries named. None demonstrates improved learning, satisfaction, access or regulatory compliance.

14.5.1.1 Example 1: a multilingual course in Germany
Suppose a business school wants to run P1 in a class using two languages of instruction. The teaching team has source cards but has not yet approved an AI service or checked the translated assessment terminology.
A proposed first step is to have a suitable reviewer check both language versions against the same capability and criteria. Until the institution approves an AI route and its data handling, learners use the fixed records and feedback. Locating a provider in Europe would not, by itself, establish compliance.
Before a pilot, the team must agree who can assess both language versions, what students may submit and how records will be handled. After an actual pilot, it could inspect disagreements in marking, independent-task evidence and access problems. Those observations are not supplied here.


14.5.1.2 Example 2: disagreement in a Singapore seminar
Suppose a business educator in Singapore wants students to question P1-F’s confident feedback. In this invented class, some learners prefer a private written response before discussing disagreement aloud. This is a supplied class constraint, not a description of Singaporean students generally.
The educator could let everyone annotate P1-F individually, then compare one decision with a partner before choosing whether to contribute to the group. Credit would depend on the source-backed explanation, not on public confidence or willingness to oppose an authority figure.
The pilot question is whether learners can identify the unsupported April warning and explain their response under the stated conditions. The educator would also ask which participation routes were usable. No gain in engagement or learning is assumed from the proposed format.


14.5.1.3 Example 3: intermittent connectivity in Nigeria
Suppose a Nigerian business school plans an S1 supplier activity where some learners share phones and the room’s internet connection is unreliable. These are fictional local conditions, not a national infrastructure assessment.
The educator could distribute a compact print sheet containing every offer, the quantity, deadline and budget. Learners calculate costs and capacity before comparing a fixed recommendation. A digital copy provides the same inputs; neither route requires a personal account or a live model.
Before teaching, check printing costs, readable layout and whether every learner can obtain the materials. During an actual pilot, record missing inputs, arithmetic errors, completion obstacles and staff time. If either route excludes learners, revise access arrangements before expansion. The scenario does not establish that a mobile-first approach improves educational quality.
crumbs: 14  Adapting to a Different Teaching Context

title: 14  Adapting to a Different Teaching Context
text:
14.6 Activity: adapt one constraint
Allow 15 minutes; no AI required. Change one condition in the pilot: unreliable connectivity, a different language of instruction or a different institutional data policy. Identify what must change, what capability remains the same and who needs to review the adaptation.
A sound answer names a practical route and a remaining check. “Ask AI to make it culturally appropriate” is a proposal for another output, not evidence that the adaptation works.
