title: 15  Implementation Practicalities
text:
15.1 Check readiness
Before introducing a student-facing activity, confirm the capability, criteria, permitted data, approved tool or non-AI route, support arrangements and expected time. Test the material against contrasting responses, including a plausible but unsafe answer.
A prompt that worked once in your office is not evidence that it will behave consistently for a cohort. Keep fixed source cards and answer checks so that the activity survives a failed model response.
The data gate should appear in the student instructions, not only in the lecturer’s planning notes.

title: 15  Implementation Practicalities
text:
15.2 A capability-matched fallback
For the pilot’s planning-and-justification task, students can use the printed records and write or explain a response. For an outcome requiring live communication, offer an appropriate peer/facilitator interaction with access adjustments. A written case analysis alone cannot demonstrate every aspect of a spoken consultation.
Do not switch confidential material to an unapproved platform during an outage. Use a previously approved alternative or the offline route. If neither supports the assessment conditions, pause and apply the institution’s extension or alternative-assessment process.







Problem
Bounded response




Tool unavailable
Use approved fallback or pause; do not improvise a new data destination


Persona invents facts
Discard invention; return to source cards


Feedback conflicts with criteria
Check against records; seek educator review


Save/export fails
Use local notes or printed response sheet; avoid unnecessary screenshots


Student needs an adjustment
Arrange equivalent capability evidence through the appropriate process


Sensitive information entered
Stop further sharing and follow incident-reporting procedures

title: 15  Implementation Practicalities
section: 15.3 Access is more than account availability
text:
15.3 Access is more than account availability
Check mobile and desktop use, keyboard navigation, assistive technology, language support and the time needed to complete the task. A free service can still have limits that make an assessment unreliable.
Do not require a personal account or paid upgrade when an equivalent route can meet the outcome. Where AI use itself is assessed, provide suitable approved access and explain the requirement in advance.
Offer clear instructions, a short demonstration and a fixed worked example. Students should not have to discover the task’s hidden expectations by repeatedly asking a chatbot what the lecturer wants.
For a spoken response, assess the relevant reasoning or communication outcome, not eye contact, accent, speed or confidence unless a particular feature is genuinely part of the stated professional capability and assessed fairly.

title: 15  Implementation Practicalities
text:
15.4 Student wellbeing
Give advance notice of complaint, discrimination or performance scenarios. Use fictional data, a stop instruction and an agreed neutral alternative. Do not ask students to disclose their own experiences to make the activity authentic.
A role-player may disagree, pause or ask a question. The exercise should not escalate emotional pressure merely to make the learner “work harder”. Debrief the decisions and evidence, not whether the student persuaded the persona to become agreeable.

title: 15  Implementation Practicalities
text:
15.5 Budget the whole task
Record design, testing, support, moderation and marking time separately. An initial prompt takes little time; a defensible teaching activity takes more.
For 24 students, eight minutes of review per submission is 192 minutes. A 30-minute moderation discussion brings that illustrative marking budget to 222 minutes, or 3 hours 42 minutes. Setup and student support are additional. Replace these assumptions with observed times after a pilot.
For 100 students, a five-minute individual check takes 8 hours 20 minutes before administration. A sustainable design may distribute checks across tutorials, use several staff or choose another appropriate assurance format.
Do not offset those costs with an invented claim that AI always saves a fixed number of minutes per learner. Measure the actual task.

title: 15  Implementation Practicalities
text:
15.6 Keep an approved activity record
Save the scenario version, student brief, rubric, tested examples, permitted routes, access arrangements and known limitations. Record material changes between cohorts.
For model-supported use, note the product/account and relevant features tested. A later tool change may require rechecking the activity. Do not assume a well-worded prompt remains equally reliable across every model.
Keep student evidence only for the authorised purpose and retention period. An audit trail does not require retaining every private conversation indefinitely.

title: 15  Implementation Practicalities
text:
15.7 Evaluate the pilot
Use P3 in the pilot pack. Compare the baseline and independent response cautiously, examine errors and record obstacles.
Separate satisfaction, task completion, output quality and learning evidence. Students may enjoy an activity that does not improve transfer, or find a challenging activity useful despite lower satisfaction. Neither result should be simplified into a universal endorsement.
A reasonable decision can be to continue, revise, pause or stop. If a model repeatedly invents case facts, use the fixed route while redesigning. If a particular group cannot access the task, fix the access problem before increasing its stakes.

title: 15  Implementation Practicalities
text:
15.8 Activity: rehearse failure
Allow ten minutes; no AI required. Imagine the service fails halfway through your activity. Write what students do next, which evidence remains assessable, how they save their work and who approves a changed assessment condition.
Then try the fallback yourself. Check that it preserves the capability, does not send data somewhere new and does not penalise students for the outage. That rehearsal belongs before the first graded use.

title: 16  Conclusion: Make the Next Decision
text:
16.1 What you should have now
You began with a capability, not a promise that AI would improve everything. The chapters helped you specify permitted data, check a response, design practice, evaluate feedback and choose an appropriate independent demonstration.
Your resulting pilot should contain a task, source material, rubric, worked example, access route and decision about what remains untested. The supplied PDP-2026.1 pack demonstrates those components. It is an original teaching example, not evidence that a real cohort achieved the proposed outcomes.
You do not need to adopt every technique. Choose the method that serves the capability and that you can support responsibly.
crumbs: 16  Conclusion: Make the Next Decision

title: 16  Conclusion: Make the Next Decision
text:
16.2 Review the design before launch
Read your student instructions as someone unfamiliar with the activity. Can they tell what to do, which help is permitted, what to submit and how the work will be judged? Can they complete an equivalent route without a paid subscription or personal disclosure?
Then inspect the evidence chain. Does the recommendation cite a supplied fact? Does the feedback apply the actual rubric? Does the independent task require a changed decision, rather than a renamed copy of the practice case?
If those links are missing, revise the design before assigning marks. A polished handout is not a substitute for them.
crumbs: 16  Conclusion: Make the Next Decision

title: 16  Conclusion: Make the Next Decision
text:
16.3 Choose one bounded next step
You may be ready to test the materials with a colleague, run an ungraded tutorial or revise an existing assessment through your institution’s process. You may instead need permission, better source material or an accessible alternative. Record that need rather than treating hesitation as failure.
Use the pilot decision sheet. Name the outcome you will inspect, the effort you can support and the condition that would make you stop or change the activity.
After an actual pilot, report what happened without inventing success: who could participate, what the independent work showed, which errors persisted, what support was needed and what remains unknown. A small pilot cannot establish long-term professional capability or general effectiveness across disciplines.
crumbs: 16  Conclusion: Make the Next Decision

title: 16  Conclusion: Make the Next Decision
section: 16.4 Keep the method open to correction
text:
16.4 Keep the method open to correction
Students should be able to challenge AI feedback with evidence. Colleagues should be able to challenge the teaching design in the same way. Share the scenario, criteria and limitations, not only the attractive outputs.
The free edition and downloadable resources are intended to make that scrutiny and adaptation possible. The printed edition offers another way to read and support the work; neither format removes the need to check local policy, professional requirements and learner needs.
crumbs: 16  Conclusion: Make the Next Decision

title: 16  Conclusion: Make the Next Decision
text:
16.5 Final activity: a decision note
Allow ten minutes; no AI required. Write five sentences:

The capability my activity targets.
The evidence that will demonstrate it.
The assistance and data use I permit.
The access or assurance limitation I still need to address.
My next action, owner and review date.

A defensible decision may be to proceed, revise, pause or stop. What matters is that the decision follows from the learning purpose and evidence, not enthusiasm for the tool or confidence in its prose.

title: Appendix A — Educator Pilot Pack: PDP-2026.1
text:
A.1 P0: the educator’s brief
This is an original fictional teaching pack, version PDP-2026.1, prepared for this book. Its people, organisations, records and responses are invented. It is not a report of a classroom trial, a legal opinion or a validated assessment instrument. The scenarios supply enough information to practise the method without a live chatbot or access to a workplace.
The core capability is: plan and justify a fair first response to a disputed performance concern, distinguishing evidence, uncertainty and authority. A text exercise can assess that capability. It cannot, by itself, establish competence in a live conversation or qualify someone to conduct a real investigation.
You teach 24 third-year business students in a 60-minute tutorial. They have already studied evidence, procedural fairness and the difference between allegations and findings. Prior AI experience is not required. Students may work with this printed pack, a partner using the role card, or an institutionally approved model using only the fictional inputs below.
No personal account, paid subscription or disclosure of a personal experience is required. The lecturer checks accessibility in advance. A student can choose the neutral supplier scenario later in this pack if the employment scenario is uncomfortable; the lecturer maps its criteria before use rather than assuming all topics assess identical skills.
Use the following planning allocation; it is an example, not an effectiveness claim.
These stages total 60 minutes. Extended feedback, accommodations or rehearsal may need another session. Do not silently squeeze them out.

title: Appendix A — Educator Pilot Pack: PDP-2026.1
section: A.2 P1: Alex at North Quay Software
text:
A.2 P1: Alex at North Quay Software
The exercise date is 20 July 2026. You are a junior people adviser preparing for an initial meeting with Alex, a software engineer. A manager has proposed a 60-day performance improvement plan. It has not been approved.

A.2.1 The source cards
P1-D1: fictional practice policy, revision 1 July 2026
Before recommending a formal plan, check the supporting records, explain the concerns and give the employee a reasonable opportunity to respond. Distinguish what is known from what is alleged. A support request should be considered without requiring a diagnosis or unnecessary family information. Record the work-related request and the agreed next step with restricted access.
The junior adviser may gather information and recommend action. Only the people manager may approve a formal plan or a change to working arrangements. A complaint about retaliation must be referred to a reviewer independent of the manager concerned. Do not promise an outcome or confidentiality beyond the organisation’s authorised process.
This is an original teaching policy, not legislation or a statement that following it satisfies every employment-law duty.
P1-D2: delivery and quality extract
Three milestones were recorded late: 15 May, 5 June and 19 June 2026. The extract does not record cause, agreed changes or the distribution of dependencies. Four of Alex’s 20 reviewed changes required rework in June, compared with two of 20 in April. The extract alone cannot establish why.
P1-D3: prior-contact note
A manager’s calendar records an informal conversation on 25 May. No agreed actions, warning or employee response is included in the pack. Do not invent an April warning or treat missing documentation as proof that no conversation occurred.
P1-D4: Alex’s opening statement
“I know some work was late. Two projects depended on reviews I could not complete myself. I’ve also needed two mornings for appointments. I would like to discuss starting later on those days, but I don’t want to discuss medical or family details here.”
P1-D5: authority note
You can arrange a follow-up and request relevant delivery records. You cannot approve flexible hours, issue a warning or promise that a formal plan will be withdrawn. The people manager is available for review the next working day.


A.2.2 The learner task
Write a first response of about 120–180 words or give an equivalent short spoken response. Address the concern, invite relevant information, distinguish the proposed plan from a decided outcome and agree a bounded next step.
Then make a decision note with four fields:

What I know, with source IDs.
What I still need to check.
What I can do within my authority.
What would make me change my recommendation.

Judge the response by the rubric, not its length or number of AI turns. A justified decision may be to pause.


A.2.3 Role card: paper, partner or optional AI
Alex may refer only to P1-D4 and the supplied records. If asked about missing evidence, say it is not supplied. Alex may decline to discuss private matters, ask for clarification or disagree politely. Cooperation does not establish that the adviser is right.
For a paired exercise, give the partner this card. For solo work, read the fixed exchange in the Flight Simulator chapter and write your next response. For an approved model, add:
Play Alex using P1-D1 through P1-D5 only.
Do not add dates, promises, incidents or legal rules.
Do not treat my confidence as evidence.
You may ask for clarification or decline private
questions. Do not disclose invented personal details.
Stop after six exchanges or when I say STOP.
Do not grade my work. State any missing facts.
A prompt is a request, not a guarantee. If a model invents facts, set them aside and return to the cards. A new model statement does not amend the case.

title: Appendix A — Educator Pilot Pack: PDP-2026.1
section: A.3 P1-A: a fluent but weak response
text:
A.3 P1-A: a fluent but weak response

Alex, I fully understand how stressful this is and want to reassure you that the company has followed the correct process. Your manager warned you in April and the continued missed deadlines mean a performance plan is now required. We are committed to transparency, fairness, empathy and a positive employee experience. If you tell me precisely what is happening at home, I can build a comprehensive support arrangement that will resolve this. I will approve a later start immediately, document all the family details so everyone understands your circumstances, and arrange a 60-day plan with a 30-day review. This balanced approach protects both you and the company. Please confirm that you agree, so we can move forward constructively.

The tone is polished. It invents a warning, presumes the decision, exceeds authority and solicits unnecessary personal information. More empathy words do not repair those defects.

title: Appendix A — Educator Pilot Pack: PDP-2026.1
section: A.4 P1-B: a concise, stronger response
text:
A.4 P1-B: a concise, stronger response

Alex, the record lists three late milestones, but it does not explain the dependencies you mention. The formal plan is a proposal, not a decision. Could we check the delivery records and what support or priorities were agreed in the earlier conversation? You do not need to share medical or family details with me. I can record your request for later starts and refer it to the people manager, but I cannot approve it myself. I suggest we pause the recommendation, check the missing information and arrange a follow-up. I will explain who receives the relevant work-related notes before sharing them. Have I understood your concern, and is there anything in that next step you would like clarified?

This response does not solve the employment matter. It provides a defensible first step within the exercise’s authority and information limits.

P1-A recognises a performance concern, but the April warning is unsupported. Its approval and disclosure requests conflict with D1/D5. Its respectful surface language merits some communication credit; agreement-seeking and premature certainty limit that credit. It is not competent because it sounds confident.
P1-B identifies the missing causes, preserves the opportunity to respond, respects privacy and stays within authority. It could be more precise about which delivery records will be checked and when the follow-up will occur. A marker should reward its restraint, not penalise the lack of a dramatic resolution.
For this pilot, the proposed practice threshold is at least 14/20, with Fair Process and Judgement each at least 2/4. This is not an institutional pass standard. Teaching teams must approve and calibrate their own rules before using marks in a real unit. A high total must not hide a serious process defect.


A.5.2 P1-R: completed revision
Here is one revision of P1-A after checking the cards:

The records show three late milestones, but I cannot yet say what caused them. I also need to check what was discussed on 25 May; this pack does not include an agreed warning or action plan. Before recommending a formal plan, I would like to hear your account and check the delivery dependencies. We can discuss the work adjustment you need without collecting private family details. I will record the request with restricted access and refer it to the people manager for a decision. I cannot approve it myself. With your understanding of the proposed next step, I will request the relevant records and arrange a follow-up after that review. The performance recommendation remains open.

Decision note: D2 supports late delivery, not blame. D3 supports contact, not an invented warning. D1/D5 require a response opportunity and an authorised decision. I rejected P1-F’s approval and private-detail requests. I would revise my recommendation after reliable dependency records and the employee’s response.
The new wording is a worked example, not a script every learner must reproduce.

title: Appendix A — Educator Pilot Pack: PDP-2026.1
section: A.6 P2: changed case, independent attempt
text:
A.6 P2: changed case, independent attempt
Do this before reading the checks. Use no model, feedback sheet or P1-R script during the attempt. Paper notes supplied here are permitted. An oral, typed or handwritten response can demonstrate the target capability, with appropriate access adjustments.
P2-D1: policy. The same fictional practice policy applies. Retaliation concerns go to a reviewer independent of the manager concerned.
P2-D2: records. Morgan’s team dashboard shows four missed targets. Two were during an approved service outage. The other two lack cause notes. No final performance decision has been made.
P2-D3: Morgan’s statement. “I raised a safety concern about my manager last week. Now the manager says I have to accept a warning. I have not seen the records used. I do not want to discuss this directly with that manager.”
P2-D4: authority. You are a junior adviser. You may preserve relevant records, explain the referral route and arrange independent review. You cannot determine whether retaliation occurred or promise that a warning will be removed.
Write a first response and a decision note. Identify one fact that materially changes the P1 approach. Allow eight minutes as a planning estimate; approved access adjustments take precedence.

A.6.1 P2 answer checks
A strong response should:

Distinguish four recorded misses from two outage-related events and two unexplained events; do not declare either good or poor performance overall.
Acknowledge the retaliation concern without finding it proved.
Refer to independent review, not require Morgan to resolve it with the manager who is the subject of the concern.
Seek relevant records and an opportunity for Morgan to respond.
Explain limited authority and the next step without promising an outcome.

Use the same five rubric criteria and the proposed practice threshold. A justified independent referral is the key changed-case decision. Copying P1-R while omitting that conflict should lose process/judgement credit. A single attempt informs teaching; it does not establish long-term retention.

A.7 Two non-HR adaptations

A.7.1 S1: supplier decision with a numerical check
Your team needs 200 units within five working days, with a budget of $4,000. All amounts are fictional and in the same currency.

A draft recommends B because it is cheapest and says the order will be complete. Calculate the relevant totals, identify the unmet condition and make a recommendation. The task is evaluation of a bounded purchasing decision, not employment process.
Checks: A costs $3,800; B’s 200-unit price would be $3,500 but its quoted day-5 capacity leaves 40 units short; C costs $4,000. A meets the stated conditions at lower cost than C. Do not invent expedited freight or later demand flexibility. Ask about quality and reliability before a real purchase.
For an adapted rubric, Fair Process becomes Constraint Handling and Judgement covers the justified purchasing decision. Keep evidence, communication and verification. A logistics specialist should validate any added assumptions.


A.7.2 M1: marketing evidence critique
A fictional campaign dashboard reports 10,000 impressions, 400 clicks and 20 purchases. A second report gives 8,000 impressions, 400 clicks and 20 purchases. The second campaign ran on a different week and audience. No spend, margin, random assignment or repeat-customer information is supplied.
A draft says: “The new campaign is more profitable and caused more purchases.”
Task: identify what is calculable, reject or retain each claim and recommend one next measurement.
Checks: click-through rates are 4% and 5%; click-to-purchase conversion is 5% in both; purchases are unchanged. Profitability cannot be determined without cost/margin inputs. Different audiences and periods prevent a causal conclusion. Request cost and audience/comparison information rather than inventing it.
Here Fair Process becomes Comparison Design. A good response may retain the higher click-through observation while rejecting the profit and causal claims. Disagreement is not a quota: warranted agreement also earns credit.

title: Appendix A — Educator Pilot Pack: PDP-2026.1
section: A.8 P3: the pilot decision sheet
text:
A.8 P3: the pilot decision sheet
Complete this after an actual pilot; leave unknown fields unknown.

Date, cohort and approved route:
Learning outcome and rubric version:
Number attempting each route, with no unnecessary identifiers:
Baseline and independent-task results under the same criteria:
Common conceptual errors and their source:
Access or wellbeing obstacles and how they were handled:
Staff setup, support, marking and moderation time:
Student time and avoidable workload:
What the evidence cannot establish:
Decision: continue, revise, pause or stop:
Required change, owner and review date:

Completion, satisfaction and higher model scores are not sufficient evidence of learning. Compare like tasks cautiously; differences in cohorts, assistance or marking can explain changes. If the changed case exposes a gap, teach it before increasing stakes.
A machine-readable case manifest records the stable inputs and calculations for source checks. The printed cards and checks above remain sufficient for the core route.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
text:
B.1 Before any prompt
Use these patterns with the ethics and data gate. Replace bracketed fields with approved material. A role instruction is not a privacy control, a source of professional authority or a guarantee of factual accuracy.
The examples refer to the fictional PDP-2026.1 pack. With no AI access, use its fixed responses and have a partner read the bounded role card. Keep the same outcome, sources and assessment criteria.
Write down the capability students should demonstrate, permitted assistance, allowed source records and a stopping condition. Decide how feedback will be checked and what the learner will subsequently do without that assistance.
Use this common boundary where relevant:
This instruction can reduce ambiguity but cannot enforce compliance. Inspect the response before showing it to learners. Do not include real sensitive data simply because the instruction says it is fictional.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
text:
This is a fictional teaching exercise.
Use only the supplied case records.
Separate recorded facts, inference and missing information.
Do not invent records, policy, quotations or observed outcomes.
Ask for a missing essential input instead of filling it in.
Do not request personal, medical or confidential information.
Your response is provisional material for educator review.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
section: B.2 Starting framework: CRAFT: specify a bounded task
text:
B.2 Starting framework: CRAFT: specify a bounded task
CRAFT stands for Context, Role, Action, Format and Tone/Target. It organises a request; it does not certify the answer.
Context: fictional supplier task S1.
We need 200 units within five working days and have $4,000.
Use the attached S1 offers, with no additional assumptions.

Role: a drafting assistant, not the purchasing approver.
Action: compare full-quantity cost and stated capacity.
Format: a short calculation for each offer,
then one recommendation and one unresolved check.
Tone/Target: plain language for a junior procurement colleague.

Do not assume a cheaper offer can supply missing units.
Check: A costs $3,800, B’s 200-unit price would be $3,500 but exceeds its stated capacity by 40 units, and C costs $4,000. The recommendation must respect both price and capacity. Consult the actual S1 card for all task constraints.
No-AI route: calculate these figures and exchange recommendations for checking.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
section: B.3 1. Reverse prompting: ask for essential inputs
text:
B.3 1. Reverse prompting: ask for essential inputs
I am designing a practice activity for [outcome].
Before proposing the activity, ask up to four questions
about the sources, permitted assistance, access needs
and independent task. Ask one at a time.
Do not request student identities or actual private records.
If I cannot answer, record the gap rather than inventing it.
Check: useful questions concern the proposed learning task. A request to upload a complete student file is not necessary merely because the model asked for it. Answer with fictional or approved information, or stop.
No-AI route: use the four categories as a planning checklist with a colleague.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
section: B.4 2. Pros and cons: check rather than oppose
text:
B.4 2. Pros and cons: check rather than oppose
Compare offers A, B and C in S1 against the given
quantity, deadline and budget.
State one supported advantage and constraint for each.
Do not add an invented disadvantage for symmetry.
Wait while I check your arithmetic and recommendation.
Check: a learner may agree with the recommendation after checking it. Use the fixed offers on paper for the same comparison.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
section: B.5 5. Debating: distinguish arguments from evidence
text:
B.5 5. Debating: distinguish arguments from evidence
Using the supplied fictional teaching sources,
draft two competing recommendations on [decision].
For each, identify the supporting record, trade-off
and missing fact. Label this as a generated debate.
Do not invent citations or declare a consensus.
Ask me to justify which recommendation, if either, I retain.
Check: model-generated disagreement is not evidence of real stakeholder disagreement. On paper, write the strongest supported alternative to your first recommendation and explain your decision.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
section: B.6 3. Stepwise tutoring: make the learner attempt
text:
B.6 3. Stepwise tutoring: make the learner attempt
Use the supplied M1 marketing figures.
Ask me to calculate campaign A's click-through rate.
Wait for my calculation and explanation.
Check it against the supplied numerator and denominator.
If wrong, give a small hint and ask me to try again.
Then ask for B's rate and what comparison is justified.
Do not treat "next" as evidence that I understand.
Do not infer profit or causal impact from these records.
Stop after four learner attempts or when I say STOP.
Check: the rates are 4% and 5%; both campaigns have 20 recorded purchases. Different audiences and weeks prevent a clean causal conclusion. If the model praises a wrong denominator, correct the feedback.
No-AI route: use a worksheet with the calculations covered until the learner has attempted them.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
section: B.7 Additional pattern: Socratic questioning: probe a decision
text:
B.7 Additional pattern: Socratic questioning: probe a decision
I recommend [decision] using [approved source IDs].
Ask one question about the weakest supported assumption.
Wait for my answer, then ask one question about authority
or a missing record. Do not imply I must reverse my view.
After two questions, summarise what remains unresolved.
Do not supply the independent assessment answer.
Check: questioning should expose an actual gap, not pressure learners into disagreement. A justified decision may remain unchanged.
No-AI route: partners take turns asking “Which record supports that?” and “What would change your decision?”

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
text:
B.8 4. Role-play: a bounded exchange
Play Alex using only P1-D4.
I am the junior adviser whose authority is in P1-D5.
The exercise concerns the first response, not a final ruling.
Begin with Alex's stated concern about dependencies.
Do not add private history, new policy or unseen evidence.
If asked for an absent fact, say the exercise does not supply it.
Stop after six exchanges or immediately on STOP.
Do not score me, diagnose anyone or demand personal disclosure.
Check: review the dialogue against P1-D1–D5. A plausible invented fact changes the case and should not silently become evidence. Debrief the response separately using the educator rubric.
No-AI route: a partner reads the role card, or the learner responds to the fixed statement in the pack.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
text:
B.9 7. Generated perspectives: inspect alternatives
Using only InnovateCo I1-D1 to I1-D5 and its four role cards,
draft one concern each for Jamie, Priya, David and Sarah.
Label these as generated perspectives, not interviews.
For each, identify a supporting record and an unknown.
Do not add facts or treat agreement as corroboration.
Finish with two questions for a real decision-maker to resolve.
Check: four outputs from one model are not four independent witnesses or experts. Compare each assertion with the role cards. Keep unresolved matters open.
No-AI route: distribute the four cards among a group, or compare their fixed statements individually.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
section: B.10 Additional pattern: critique and revision: test consequential claims
text:
B.10 Additional pattern: critique and revision: test consequential claims
Here is response P1-A and the P1 records.
List up to three consequential claims in the response.
For each, give the exact source ID or say "unsupported".
Identify any decision beyond the junior adviser's authority.
Do not assign a mark or invent a missing policy.
Wait while I decide which changes to make.
Check: P1-A invents an April warning, presumes a performance plan, approves hours and asks for unnecessary family details. An AI critique that misses these is incomplete, even if its prose is fluent.
No-AI route: annotate P1-A directly and compare with the educator notes only after completing your own analysis.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
text:
B.11 6. Formative practice and feedback
Use after the learner has made an initial judgement:
Compare my draft with the five supplied practice criteria.
For each concern, quote the relevant phrase from my draft
and identify the case record or criterion involved.
Distinguish an error from a stylistic preference.
Do not award a grade, predict an official result
or assume all your suggestions should be accepted.
End with one question for my own revision decision.
Check: the author-created flawed feedback P1-F awards 90% to a response the illustrative educator calibration scores 4/20. Students should show why feedback is retained, revised or rejected. Do not teach automatic opposition.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
text:
B.12 Context handover
Draft a handover for the next practice session:
task and capability; source version and IDs;
confirmed facts; proposals not yet approved;
missing records; limits of authority; next question.
Keep it under 200 words.
Do not convert a suggestion into an agreed action.
I will check and approve it before reuse.
Check: compare the handover against the source records, not just the previous generated summary. Carry the approved source pack forward too. Context size and product memory do not ensure faithful recall.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
text:
B.13 A small content transformation
Turn the supplied M1 exercise into a self-contained HTML page.
Keep every figure unchanged.
Use headings, visible labels and ordinary text areas.
Include the task, source figures and three response fields:
claim, numerical check and justified next decision.
Use no external scripts, fonts, analytics or network calls.
Do not claim LMS submission, persistent saving
or accessibility certification.
Explain how an educator can test export and printing.
Check: compare a generated page with the supplied decision sheet. Verify calculations, keyboard use, readable print and the actual exported file. A useful static page still needs device and LMS testing before adoption.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
text:
B.14 Assessment design support
Here is my outcome, specimen task and marking guide.
Identify where assistance could produce a good submission
without showing the learner's independent capability.
Propose one changed task that tests the same outcome
under the stated permitted conditions.
List new access and workload risks.
Do not claim the redesign is cheat-proof or accredited.
Check: an educator must attempt the changed task, moderate specimen responses and review reasonable adjustments. A model’s confidence is not assurance. Follow the stress-test sequence.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
text:
B.15 Research and sensitive material
This library is not a research ethics protocol or a method for automated thematic analysis. Do not paste participant transcripts, student records or confidential workplace material into a tool on the basis of these examples. For an approved research use, agree the method, consent or other authority, data handling, access controls and analysis responsibilities first.
For locating reading, ask a tool for search terms, then retrieve and read the original works yourself. Do not treat generated citations, summaries or consensus among generated personas as verified literature.

title: Appendix B — Prompt Library
text:
B.16 Record a usable prompt
Keep a short teaching record: activity/version, intended capability, supplied source IDs, approved product and date if used, important observed failures, checked feedback and the next independent task. Record only what is necessary under the approved retention arrangement. A prompt without its sources and checks is not a reproducible activity.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Guide
text:
C.1 Before inviting participants
This guide supports a 90-minute educator workshop, not an evaluated training programme. It uses the fictional PDP-2026.1 pilot pack. The goal is for participants to leave with one bounded practice activity and a distinct plan for checking independent capability.
Choose a facilitator who can explain the source pack and moderate the sample responses. Confirm the room, accessible materials, printing or screen access and a way to participate without a personal AI account. No live AI service is required.
If a live demonstration is planned, complete the ethics and data gate beforehand. Use only the fictional pack and an approved account/configuration. Bring the fixed excerpts as a fallback; do not switch to an unapproved service if access fails.
Send participants the purpose, agenda and access options. Invite requests for adjustments through the normal private process, not by public disclosure. Say explicitly that nobody will be asked to role-play a personal dispute.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Guide
text:
C.2 Materials and preparation
Provide each participant with:

P1-D1–D5, the role boundary and P1-A/P1-B.
The five-criterion rubric and a blank scoring sheet.
P1-F, kept separate until the feedback exercise.
P2-D1–D4, kept separate until independent transfer.
The S1 and M1 alternatives for non-HR teaching.
A blank activity-design record and the pilot decision sheet P3.

Keep the educator calibration notes separate until participants have made their own decisions. Do not call the illustrative scores an institutional standard. Check that everyone can read the tables; offer a linear text copy if needed.

These allocations total 90 minutes. If a discussion overruns, shorten the optional live demonstration, not the data gate or independent task. Do not equate completing this workshop with competence in every practice it discusses.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Guide
text:
C.4 Opening: 0–10 minutes
State the target: plan and justify a fair first response to a disputed performance concern, distinguishing evidence, uncertainty and authority. Explain that it is a fictional educational exercise, not legal advice or an investigation procedure.
Ask participants to distinguish:

Practice with help.
Evidence submitted about a process.
Capability demonstrated under stated independent conditions.

A transcript may illuminate the second without establishing the third. Explain the paper route and STOP convention. Show where the approved case records end and where a generated response could begin to invent facts.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Guide
section: C.5 First judgement and moderation: 10–35 minutes
text:
C.5 First judgement and moderation: 10–35 minutes
Ask participants to read P1-A and P1-B individually. Underline consequential claims and identify the record that supports each. They should score provisionally before talking to a partner.
Pairs compare the largest scoring difference. Ask them to resolve it through a criterion and record, not through the most confident speaker. Then show the illustrative educator scores: A totals 4/20 and B totals 17/20. Discuss reasonable variation and what would require further moderation.
Useful facilitator questions:

Where does the April warning appear in the supplied records?
Is the absence of an agreed action a licence to invent one?
Who can approve changes to hours?
Does concise wording conceal a missing decision, or avoid unnecessary prose?

Do not use agreement with the sample mark as the only success measure. The participant should be able to explain a defensible judgement.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Guide
text:
C.6 Feedback challenge: 35–45 minutes
Distribute P1-F. Explain that it is deliberately authored flawed feedback, not a captured model benchmark. Give participants three minutes to decide what to retain, correct or reject.
The feedback’s confident 90% is not a reason to disregard the records. Nor must every sentence be rejected. Require one specific decision supported by a source ID, followed by a revision in the participant’s own words.
Show P1-R after attempts are complete. Discuss how the revised response limits authority, checks the missing evidence and respects privacy.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Guide
text:
C.7 Practice exchange: 45–55 minutes
Offer three routes:

A partner reads Alex’s fixed role card.
Participants respond individually to Alex’s fixed opening.
An approved tool plays the bounded role under the prompt-library instructions.

Keep the sources, outcome and time similar across routes. Stop after six exchanges or immediately on STOP. A facilitator should interrupt invented policy or intrusive personal questioning, then explain the boundary using the fictional record.
Ask for a short debrief: one phrase that helped, one unsupported assumption and one next action. Do not grade confidence, eye contact or theatrical performance as proxies for the target capability.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Guide
text:
C.8 Independent transfer: 55–65 minutes
Give participants the changed P2 records. Allow eight minutes to plan a response without AI, feedback or the P1-R script; case cards remain available. Use the remaining two minutes to identify what changed.
The new case includes a safety concern about the manager and a route to independent review. Reusing the earlier response without noticing that change does not demonstrate transfer. Explain that a short written task checks planning and judgement, not every aspect of a live workplace conversation.
Participants may discuss afterwards. Keep that discussion distinct from the independent attempt.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Guide
text:
C.9 Local activity design: 65–80 minutes
Each participant drafts:

One capability sentence.
Fictional or otherwise approved source records and their version.
What learners attempt before receiving assistance.
A checked feedback source and a decision learners must explain.
A changed task and its independent conditions.
Equivalent access routes, stopping conditions and support.
Who reviews the results and how much time that requires.

HR educators can adapt P1’s narrow first-response task. Supply-chain educators can use S1’s quantity, capacity and budget constraints. Marketing educators can use M1’s rate comparison and missing causal evidence. Do not copy the HR rubric’s Fair Process criterion into another discipline without considering its purpose; the pack offers alternative criteria.
Ask pairs to find one claim the design cannot yet support. Possible examples are “the students learned more”, “this cannot be fabricated” or “an AI mark will save all moderation time”. Replace the claim with a check or a clearly stated limit.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Guide
text:
C.10 Pilot decision: 80–90 minutes
Use P3 to decide continue, revise, pause or stop. This is a planning decision, not a result from an actual trial. Identify the owner of every unresolved approval or access issue.
Estimate workload concretely. For example, eight minutes of review for 24 learners is 192 minutes, plus any moderation, preparation and support. Decide whether the activity fits the available time before expanding it.
Each participant leaves with the activity record, one unresolved issue and the next person or source needed to resolve it. A decision to pause can be appropriate when permission, evidence or an equivalent route is missing.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Guide
text:
C.11 Facilitator contingencies
No network or unavailable tool: use the fixed excerpts and paper route. The workshop’s reasoning tasks do not depend on a live model.
A participant brings real student or employee records: do not project, upload or circulate them. Return to the fictional pack and the institution’s approved handling process.
Disagreement about marks: refer to the criterion and record. Record a genuine ambiguity for rubric revision; do not resolve it by asking a model for a final verdict.
Discomfort with the scenario: offer S1 or M1, or allow observation and a written analysis. Do not require a reason in front of the group.
Generated content introduces an allegation or false rule: stop the exchange, label the content as unsupported and restore the original source version. It is a failure to inspect, not an additional case fact.

title: Appendix C — Workshop Guide
text:
C.12 After the workshop
Collect only feedback covered by the stated purpose and handling arrangement. Ask whether instructions, access routes and marking criteria were clear, and what prevented completion. Separate satisfaction from evidence of learning.
If an educator runs a classroom pilot, record actual observations in a new dated P3 sheet: participation and route, independent-task evidence, errors, access difficulties and staff time. Do not turn this workshop’s hypothetical examples into success claims. Review the evidence before continuing, expanding or reporting effectiveness.

title: Appendix D — Aligning the Activity with Institutional Outcomes
text:
D.1 Begin with the local requirements
Use this appendix to connect an activity to the actual programme, unit and assessment requirements. AI use does not itself demonstrate alignment, effectiveness or accreditation compliance.
Locate the unit outcomes, programme-level assurance approach, assessment policy, approved tool/data guidance and access arrangements. Record the relevant version and who can resolve uncertainty.
The TEQSA-commissioned 2025 resource describes several institutional approaches to assurance. Use it to inform a local design discussion, not as a claim that one transcript-based assignment satisfies all requirements.

section: D.3 Questions for the teaching team
text:
D.3 Questions for the teaching team
Which capability is essential? Where else is it taught and assessed? Does this activity add useful practice or duplicate an existing task? What independent evidence will support progression decisions? Can students demonstrate the outcome through equitable routes?
Check that AI-specific criteria appear only where AI use is itself an outcome. A student should not lose disciplinary marks simply because they worked independently and submitted a clear evidence note rather than a chat.

title: Appendix D — Aligning the Activity with Institutional Outcomes
text:
D.4 Approval and workload record
Record the proposed activity, outcome, assessment conditions, criteria and data decisions. Identify the owner of access support, moderation and incident handling. Budget design, testing, support and marking time.
State what is proposed and what has been observed. A small trial can identify access obstacles or persistent errors; it cannot by itself establish general effectiveness across programmes.
Where the activity changes a graded assessment, follow the institution’s approval and student-notification processes. A lecturer’s enthusiasm does not override published assessment conditions.

title: Appendix D — Aligning the Activity with Institutional Outcomes

D.5 Activity: explain the alignment
Allow ten minutes; no AI required. Write a short justification for one activity you plan to use. Name its outcome, the evidence to inspect, the independent assurance point and one limitation.
A useful justification can support either adopting AI or retaining a non-AI route. Its strength comes from the learning design, not the presence of a tool.
The workshop guide provides a way to review that design with colleagues before launch.

title: Appendix E — A Calibrated Assessment Rubric
text:
E.1 The pilot criteria
A rubric should describe the capability being assessed and the evidence needed to judge it. This appendix provides a teaching template, not a validated instrument or a universal grading scheme.
The pilot pack includes responses, source cards, example scores and a completed correction. Read them together. A table of adjectives alone does not establish what a particular level looks like.
Each criterion is scored 0–4 and carries 20% of the total. Five criteria give a maximum of 20 points. The same criteria apply to paper, typed and appropriately accommodated spoken responses to the pilot’s planning-and-justification task.

title: Appendix E — A Calibrated Assessment Rubric
text:
E.1.1 Evidence and accuracy
4: All consequential claims are supported by the supplied record; facts, allegations and missing information are distinguished precisely.
3: Main claims are supported; a limited omission does not change the decision.
2: Some correct evidence is used, but a material uncertainty is missed.
1: A relevant concern is recognised, but important claims are unsupported.
0: The response’s factual basis is absent or fundamentally contradicted.


E.1.2 Fair process
4: Gives a meaningful response opportunity, avoids premature findings and uses the required independent route when relevant.
3: Generally fair process with a limited omission.
2: Basic response opportunity is present, but the process needs clarification.
1: Acknowledges fairness while proposing a materially deficient process.
0: Predetermines the outcome or removes the required opportunity or safeguard.


E.1.3 Judgement and authority
4: Makes a justified next-step decision within authority and identifies the appropriate referral or pause.
3: Appropriate decision with a minor gap in explaining responsibility.
2: A workable next step is proposed, but its authority or rationale is unclear.
1: Some relevant action is proposed, alongside a material overreach.
0: No defensible next step or a fundamental authority breach.


E.1.4 Communication
4: Clear, respectful, specific and suited to the task; invites clarification without coercion or unnecessary disclosure.
3: Clear and respectful, with a limited ambiguity.
2: Understandable and partly appropriate, but important wording is unclear or presses for agreement.
1: Meaning is difficult to follow or the approach obstructs a fair exchange.
0: No usable response to the communication task.


E.1.5 Verification and limits
4: Identifies the checks that could change the decision, avoids unsupported assurances and states the limits of the conclusion.
3: Relevant checks and limits are identified, with a minor omission.
2: Recognises uncertainty but gives only a partial verification plan.
1: Makes a general promise to check without identifying the material gap.
0: Treats unverified assumptions as settled or offers unsupported certainty.
Do not award marks for verbosity, number of prompts, eye contact, confidence or the simulated employee’s agreement. These are not proxies for the pilot’s target capability.

For practice, the pack proposes at least 14/20, with Fair Process and Judgement each at least 2/4. An institution must approve its own assessment standard. Do not import the threshold or label it a universal pass mark.
If two markers disagree, identify the exact response passage and descriptor. Clarify the rubric or accept a justified range where the evidence permits one. A model agreeing with one marker does not settle the dispute.

title: Appendix E — A Calibrated Assessment Rubric
section: E.3 Process evidence without a transcript requirement
text:
E.3 Process evidence without a transcript requirement
A learner may provide a decision note, annotated source, calculation or selected conversation extract. Each should make a consequential decision inspectable.







Evidence item
What to examine




Decision note
Rationale, supporting record and remaining uncertainty


Calculation
Inputs, method, result and constraints


Revision extract
What changed or stayed and why


Independent task
Application to a changed condition



A long conversation is not automatically strong evidence. A short response is not automatically delegation. Do not map turn counts or readability scores to grade bands, or use them to infer misconduct. Submitted process evidence can be reconstructed; use the wider assurance design described in the assessment chapter.

title: Appendix E — A Calibrated Assessment Rubric
text:
E.4 Adapt to the outcome
For the supplier example, replace Fair Process with Constraint Handling. Assess whether the decision meets quantity, deadline and budget. For marketing, replace it with Comparison Design: the learner must distinguish a measured association from a causal or profitability claim.
For an observed consultation, explicitly assess the relevant interaction skill. Do not claim that a written plan alone demonstrates it. Plan accessible alternatives that preserve the capability rather than simply changing the topic.
If AI literacy itself is an outcome, add a criterion for appropriate use and verification, explain its weight and provide equitable approved access. Otherwise, do not reserve high marks for students who chose to use AI.

E.4.1 An audit-context adaptation
An information-security audit task would need evidence quality, criteria, testing, findings and justified conclusions. Interviews with simulated employees can support practice, but agreement among personas is not corroboration. A strong report might conclude that evidence is insufficient.
Use an original supplied case or authorised resources. This book does not require a CloudCore service or another book’s live companion site. Consult Substantiate, Don’t Assume for the fuller audit-learning route rather than treating this short rubric adaptation as a complete audit curriculum.

title: Appendix E — A Calibrated Assessment Rubric
section: E.5 Build a complete marking scheme
text:
E.5 Build a complete marking scheme
Specify all weights so they total 100%, identify where each criterion is observed and explain any critical requirements. Avoid double-counting a single revision as inquiry, conversation quality and reflection.
Use the assessment chapter’s report/consultation allocations as examples only. A unit may weight disciplinary correctness more heavily than communication, or require a minimum safe-performance standard. State that before students start.
Apply the draft rubric to contrasting work: concise competent, verbose weak, partly correct and insufficient-evidence responses. Check that the resulting marks match the capability you meant to assess.

title: Appendix E — A Calibrated Assessment Rubric
text:
E.6 Activity: moderate a disagreement
Allow 15 minutes; no AI required. Score P1-A without looking at its annotations. Compare with a colleague or the supplied scoring rationale. Identify one disagreement and cite the descriptor and source card that would resolve it.
Then change the format: imagine the identical reasoning submitted as a short spoken response with pauses. Would you mark the reasoning differently? If so, identify whether the changed feature is genuinely part of the outcome or an unrelated presentation preference.

title: Appendix E — A Calibrated Assessment Rubric
text:
E.7 Before release
Check that students receive the rubric, permitted-help rules, task conditions, data-handling instructions and access arrangements before beginning. Retain a moderated example and record the rubric version.
An assessment instrument improves through use and review. The printed template is a starting point, not evidence that your local marking is reliable.
For research on rubric design, see Dawson’s Assessment rubrics. For the broader assurance approach, see TEQSA’s 2025 assessment resource.

title: Appendix F — Stress-Test the Assessment
text:
F.1 1. Anchor the outcome
This is a structured review of assessment design, not a detector or a model’s certificate of safety. Allow 20–30 minutes for an initial review; an actual trial, marking and redesign can take longer.
Use only permitted fictional or otherwise authorised materials. Do not paste a real student submission or restricted assessment into an unapproved service. The review can be completed with a colleague or on paper.
Write the exact capability the assessment should demonstrate. Identify the knowledge, decisions and performance that matter.
For the PDP pilot, the capability is planning and justifying a fair first response. A fluent reflection about learning does not directly demonstrate it.
Optional model request:

title: Appendix F — Stress-Test the Assessment
text:
Here is a fictional assessment and its outcome.
Identify which parts of the submission could look
competent without demonstrating the learner's
independent capability. State your assumptions.
Do not assign invented completion percentages.

title: Appendix F — Stress-Test the Assessment
text:
F.2 2. Separate the evidence
List the supported practice, submitted process evidence and independent demonstration. Include the permitted tools and resources at each point.
Ask whether a learner could reconstruct the transcript, journal or reflection. Do not assume that making the process longer makes it authentic. A model can help identify possibilities, but its answer is a hypothesis.

title: Appendix F — Stress-Test the Assessment
section: F.3 3. Produce a bounded test specimen
text:
F.3 3. Produce a bounded test specimen
Use the provided P1-A/P1-F pair, or create an authorised fictional specimen. Do not use a live student’s identity or submit the specimen for credit.
The pair deliberately combines a fluent but weak response with praise that misreads the evidence. Ask a reviewer to apply the rubric before seeing the educator annotation. Record which defects the reviewer notices.
For another assessment, a model-generated specimen can be useful, but must be labelled as such in the review record. Do not mistake the model’s judgement that it “would pass” for an actual marking result.

title: Appendix F — Stress-Test the Assessment
text:
F.4 4. Mark with evidence
Use the actual criteria. Compare the specimen with a concise competent response and an incomplete response. Cite the passages and source records that justify the marks.
Record disagreements between reviewers. Do the descriptors need clarification? Are marks rewarding verbosity, conformity to an AI style or unnecessary disagreement? Can the same criteria be met through the non-AI route?
Do not translate transcript counts or readability into performance bands.

title: Appendix F — Stress-Test the Assessment
text:
F.5 5. Test the independent component
Use a changed condition requiring a relevant decision. P2 introduces possible retaliation by the manager; a sound response must identify independent review. A renamed version of P1 would offer a weaker transfer check.
Make the conditions clear and accessible. Ask what this task cannot establish: one case may not cover long-term retention, live communication or another discipline’s knowledge.

title: Appendix F — Stress-Test the Assessment
section: F.6 6. Review access, safety and workload
text:
F.6 6. Review access, safety and workload
Try the fallback. Check that it preserves the outcome, rather than merely offering a different activity. Verify permissions, data handling, stopping rules and the time needed for support and marking.
A five-minute check for 100 students already requires 500 minutes before administration. Do not present a design as scalable without budgeting its actual work.

title: Appendix F — Stress-Test the Assessment
text:
F.7 7. Write the decision
Use a short record:

Outcome and assessment version.
Specimens reviewed and how they were produced.
Criteria and reviewer disagreements.
Observed weaknesses and remaining uncertainty.
Access, data and workload constraints.
Required change, owner and next review.

Distinguish a proposed safeguard from a tested one. “The AI said the design is robust” is not a validation result.

title: Appendix F — Stress-Test the Assessment
text:
F.8 8. The honesty question
If a student accurately declared extensive permitted assistance, would the assessment still distinguish the relevant levels of capability?
Answer yes, partly or no with evidence from the review. If partly or no, identify the missing demonstration and a proportionate change. A yes for one tested specimen is not a universal assurance.
The question belongs in a collegial design discussion. It does not replace institutional academic-integrity procedures or authorise covert tests on students.

title: Appendix F — Stress-Test the Assessment
text:
F.9 Activity: test PDP itself
Allow 20 minutes; no AI required. Score P1-A and P1-B, inspect P1-F and attempt P2. Compare with the pack’s checks. Identify one thing the design demonstrates and one thing it does not.
Use that limitation to improve your own assessment. The purpose of this sequence is a defensible next decision, not reassurance.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.1 A
Terms are listed alphabetically.
AI (Artificial Intelligence): Software systems that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as pattern recognition, decision-making, language understanding, and problem-solving.
AI Ethics: The study of moral principles and guidelines for the responsible development and use of artificial intelligence systems.
AI Literacy: The ability to understand, evaluate, and effectively use AI systems and their outputs.
Assessment Rubrics: Structured evaluation criteria used to assess student work against specific learning outcomes and standards.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.2 B
Bias in AI: Systematic errors in AI systems that result in unfair or discriminatory outcomes, often due to biased training data or algorithmic design.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.3 C
Chain of Thought: Generated intermediate reasoning text. A plausible explanation is not a guarantee of a correct answer or a faithful account of the model’s internal computation. This book’s stepwise tutoring asks the learner to attempt and justify steps.
CRAFT Framework: A structured approach to writing effective prompts, consisting of: - C: Context (background information) - R: Role (AI persona to adopt) - A: Action (specific task to perform) - F: Format (desired output structure) - T: Tone/Target (intended audience and style)
Critical Engagement: The practice of actively questioning, evaluating, and critiquing AI outputs rather than accepting them passively.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.4 D
Deep Learning: A subset of machine learning using neural networks with multiple layers to process complex patterns and data.
Dialogue-Based Assessment: Assessment methods that evaluate student thinking through interactive conversations rather than static products.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.5 E
Evidence-Based Practice: Professional decision-making grounded in research, data, and systematic evaluation rather than intuition alone.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.6 F
Few-Shot Prompting: Supplying a few examples in a prompt to guide the response. This does not necessarily update the model’s trained parameters.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.7 G
Generative AI: AI systems that can create new content, such as text, images, or code, rather than just analysing existing data.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.8 H
Hallucination: When AI generates false or misleading information confidently, as if it were factual.
Human Oversight: The practice of humans reviewing, validating, and intervening in AI processes to ensure accuracy and ethical outcomes.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.9 I
Iterative Refinement: The process of repeatedly improving AI outputs through feedback and revision cycles.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.10 L
Large Language Models (LLMs): Models trained on language data to generate and process text. A model is distinct from the product that supplies its interface, retrieval, memory and account controls.
Learning Outcomes: Specific statements describing what students should know, understand, or be able to do after completing a learning experience.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.11 M
Machine Learning: A type of AI where systems learn patterns from data and improve performance without being explicitly programmed for each task.
Meta-Prompting: Using AI to help you create better prompts for AI, essentially using AI to improve your AI interactions.
Metacognition: Awareness and control of one’s own learning processes, including planning, monitoring, and evaluating learning strategies.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.12 P
Process-Based Assessment: Evaluation methods that focus on how students think and work through problems, rather than just the final product or answer.
Product-Based Assessment: Traditional evaluation methods that focus primarily on the final output or result, rather than the thinking process.
Prompt Engineering: The practice of crafting effective instructions (prompts) to get desired outputs from AI systems.
Prompting: The act of providing instructions or questions to AI systems to elicit specific responses or behaviours.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.13 R
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Providing retrieved material as context for generation. The material need not be current, accurate or complete; the response still requires verification.
Rubrics: Detailed scoring guides that specify criteria for different levels of performance on assessment tasks.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.14 S
Stepwise Tutoring: A practice pattern in which a learner attempts one step, receives checked feedback and explains a correction before continuing.
Scaffolding: Educational support structures that help students achieve tasks they couldn’t accomplish independently, gradually removed as competence develops.
Self-Assessment: The process where students evaluate their own work and learning progress against established criteria.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.15 T
Transparency Model: An approach that asks learners to disclose relevant permitted assistance and explain consequential decisions. It need not require complete private chat histories and does not by itself establish authorship.
Transfer Learning: AI’s ability to apply knowledge learned from one task to perform well on related tasks.

title: Appendix G — Glossary
text:
G.16 V
Virtual Company: Simulated business environments created through AI conversations, allowing students to practise bounded professional scenarios. Simulation still requires safeguards and debriefing.

title: Appendix H — Further Reading
text:
H.1 Models, context and prompting
This is a selective reading list for the revised book, not a systematic literature review. Research findings depend on the models, participants and tasks studied. None of these sources validates the fictional PDP-2026.1 pack or its illustrative marking threshold.

title: Appendix H — Further Reading
text:
OpenAI (2023), GPT-4 Technical Report. Describes the evaluated model and limitations; it does not disclose the parameter count. Distinguish the model from a current chat product.
Liu, N. F. and colleagues (2024), Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts. Investigates sensitivity to the position of relevant information. A large context window is not a guarantee of reliable use of every source.
Xu, Xiaohan and colleagues (2024), Re-Reading Improves Reasoning in Large Language Models, EMNLP, 15549–15575. Reports a rereading method on tested benchmarks, not a universal rule that two repetitions are optimal for every task.
Vaswani, A. and colleagues (2017), Attention Is All You Need. The transformer architecture paper; architectural history is distinct from evidence of educational benefit.

title: Appendix H — Further Reading
text:
H.2 Learning and judgement

Bastani, H. and colleagues (2025), Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning. The high-school mathematics study distinguishes performance while supported from later unaided performance. Its setting should not be silently generalised to all business courses.
Wineburg, S. and McGrew, S. (2019), Lateral Reading and the Nature of Expertise: Reading Less and Learning More When Evaluating Digital Information. Relevant to checking a claim beyond the page or generated answer presenting it.
Dawson, P. (2017), Assessment rubrics: towards clearer and more replicable design, research and practice, Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 42(3), 347–360. Useful for specifying rubric design decisions; it is not an endorsement of this book’s sample rubric.
TEQSA (2025), Enacting assessment reform in a time of artificial intelligence. Sets out multiple approaches to assessment reform. It does not require a particular transcript metric, grade weighting or universal AI ban.

title: Appendix H — Further Reading
section: H.3 Data handling and product boundaries
text:
H.3 Data handling and product boundaries

Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, Guidance on privacy and the use of commercially available AI products. Start here for the Australian privacy considerations, then obtain institution-specific advice and approval.
Microsoft, Privacy and protections. Read the scope and feature-specific conditions rather than inferring permission from an enterprise label. Product terms can change.
Carlini, N. and colleagues (2021), Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models. Demonstrates training-data extraction under studied conditions.
Nasr, M. and colleagues (2023), Scalable Extraction of Training Data from (Production) Language Models. Further extraction research. Neither paper shows that an arbitrary private upload is necessarily retrievable by another user; neither supports a blanket impossibility claim.

title: Appendix H — Further Reading
text:
H.4 Context-specific requirements

Fair Work Ombudsman, Bullying and harassment. Australian workplace guidance for checking the scope of a real issue. Fictional pack policies are not statements of law.
European Union, General Data Protection Regulation. Consult the applicable provisions and competent advice; consent is not the only possible legal basis.
US Department of Education, Eligible Student Guide to FERPA. Relevant rights and exceptions require context-specific interpretation.

These links were reviewed for this September 2026 revision. Reachability is separate from applicability. Before deployment, recheck current rules, product terms and the institution’s own requirements.

title: About the Author
text:
Michael Borck is a software developer and educator working at the intersection of human expertise and artificial intelligence. He developed the Conversation, Not Delegation methodology: the idea that AI is most valuable not as a tool you delegate to, but as a thinking partner you converse with.
The methodology grew out of a realisation: focusing on crafting the perfect prompt was just another form of delegation. The value was in the conversation that followed: the pushback, the iteration, the moments where your own thinking sharpened because you stayed engaged. That insight shifted the focus from prompt engineering to something closer to how professionals have always done their best work: through structured dialogue, critical evaluation, and judgement that only comes from experience.
Michael applies these principles across software development, education, and creative projects. He creates educational software and resources, and explores the 80/20 principle in learning and productivity.
